name: Blockchain
definition: A blockchain is a shared, append-only database maintained by many computers in a network, in which transaction data is grouped into blocks and each block cryptographically references its parent, so that altering past data requires redoing all subsequent blocks and network consensus.
intuition: Think of it as a public ledger copied onto thousands of computers: everyone holds the same history, and no single party can quietly rewrite it.
mechanics: Transactions are batched into blocks; each block contains a hash of the previous block, chaining them together. Nodes independently verify every new block against consensus rules, and a consensus mechanism (e.g. proof-of-work or proof-of-stake) decides which blocks extend the canonical chain.
failure_modes: A 51% attack or consensus failure can reorganize recent blocks, reversing transactions; software bugs in dominant client implementations can halt or split the chain.
misconceptions: Blockchains are not inherently immutable at the tip — recent blocks can be reorganized, which is why confirmations or finality matter. Not every blockchain is decentralized or permissionless; private chains exist.
example: If you send ETH to someone, the transaction is included in a block; on proof-of-stake Ethereum, after roughly two epochs (~13 minutes) the block containing it is finalized and cannot be reverted without at least one-third of staked ETH being destroyed.

name: Distributed ledger
definition: A distributed ledger is a database that is replicated, shared and synchronized across multiple nodes or institutions, with updates agreed through a consensus process rather than written by a single central administrator.
intuition: Instead of one bank keeping the master copy of the books, every participant keeps an identical copy and they all agree on each new entry.
mechanics: Each node holds a copy of the ledger; new records are propagated through the peer-to-peer network and accepted only if they satisfy the protocol's validation and consensus rules. A blockchain is one specific form of distributed ledger that orders records in cryptographically chained blocks, but DLT also includes non-block structures (e.g. DAGs, permissioned ledgers).
failure_modes: If the consensus layer or validator set is compromised or centralized in practice, the ledger can be censored or rewritten despite nominal distribution; poor network connectivity can partition the ledger into divergent views.
misconceptions: 'Distributed ledger' and 'blockchain' are not synonyms — all blockchains are DLT, but distributed ledgers need not organize data in blocks or be public. Distribution of copies does not by itself guarantee distribution of control.
example: Ethereum's ledger of accounts and smart-contract state is stored and updated by every node in the network, so two independent nodes reading the same finalized block compute the same balances without trusting each other.

name: Consensus mechanism
definition: A consensus mechanism is the complete stack of protocols, incentives and ideas that allows a distributed network of nodes to agree on a single state of a blockchain, including Sybil resistance, block author selection and a chain-selection (fork-choice) rule.
intuition: It is the rulebook that lets thousands of strangers agree on one version of history without a referee.
mechanics: A Sybil-resistance component (e.g. proof-of-work's energy expenditure or proof-of-stake's locked capital) makes it costly to fake identities; a block-production protocol selects who proposes and validates blocks; and a fork-choice rule (longest/heaviest chain) resolves competing versions. Economic rewards and penalties align honest behavior.
failure_modes: If an attacker obtains 51% of hash power or a large share of stake, they can censor or reorder transactions and, below finality thresholds, reorganize the chain; bugs in the fork-choice rule can cause chain splits.
misconceptions: Proof-of-work and proof-of-stake alone are not complete consensus mechanisms — they are Sybil-resistance and block-author-selection components inside one (e.g. Ethereum's Gasper combines Casper-FFG with LMD-GHOST).
example: On Ethereum, consensus is reached when validators representing at least two-thirds of total staked ETH attest to checkpoint blocks, at which point those checkpoints are justified and then finalized.

name: Proof of work
definition: Proof of work (PoW) is a Sybil-resistance and block-author-selection mechanism in which miners compete to find a nonce that makes a block's hash fall below a difficulty target, expending real-world computation; the chain with the most accumulated work is treated as canonical.
intuition: Miners burn electricity on a lottery; the winning ticket lets them write the next page of the ledger, and cheating would require out-computing the whole honest network.
mechanics: Miners repeatedly hash a candidate block header with different nonces until the hash meets the target set by the difficulty parameter; difficulty retargets to keep average block time constant. Validity is cheap to verify but expensive to produce, and the longest (most-work) chain rule resolves forks.
formula: Find nonce n such that H(block_header(n)) <= T, where T = target set by difficulty (lower T = harder); probability per hash ≈ T / 2^256 (SHA-256).
failure_modes: An attacker controlling a majority of hash rate can double-spend by mining a private chain that outpaces the honest one; mining-pool centralization and hardware/energy concentration erode the security model.
misconceptions: PoW does not 'solve a useful puzzle' — the computation is deliberately useless work whose only purpose is to be costly. High hash rate secures history but does not increase transaction throughput.
example: In Bitcoin, miners increment a nonce until the block hash has the required number of leading zero bits; at ~10-minute block targets, an attacker trying to reverse a 6-block-deep transaction must redo that work and then outpace all honest miners, an economically prohibitive task.

name: Proof of stake
definition: Proof of stake (PoS) is a Sybil-resistance and block-author-selection mechanism in which validators lock capital (stake) that can be destroyed (slashed) for dishonest behavior, and are pseudo-randomly selected to propose and attest to blocks.
intuition: Instead of proving you burned electricity, you post a bond: misbehave and your bond is burned, so cheating costs you directly.
mechanics: In Ethereum's PoS, a validator deposits 32 ETH, runs execution, consensus and validator clients, and is randomly selected to propose blocks in 12-second slots while committees attest each epoch. Casper-FFG finalizes checkpoints backed by ≥2/3 of staked ETH; equivocation or contradictory attestations are slashable.
failure_modes: An attacker with >1/3 of stake can stall finality, and with a majority can steer the fork choice; long-range attacks and weak subjectivity require checkpoints; staking-pool centralization can concentrate effective control.
misconceptions: PoS does not pay interest for 'locking money in a bank' — rewards pay for active validation duties, and downtime or misbehavior incurs penalties. Staked capital is not risk-free yield.
example: A user deposits 32 ETH into the Ethereum deposit contract, joins the activation queue, and then attests every epoch (~6.4 minutes); if they propose two blocks in the same slot, part of their stake is slashed and they are ejected.

name: Validator
definition: A validator is a node participant in a proof-of-stake network that has deposited stake and is responsible for checking new blocks, attesting to the head of the chain, and occasionally proposing new blocks, earning rewards for honest work and penalties or slashing for failures or misbehavior.
intuition: A validator is like a juror with money on the table: it votes on what the true chain is, and loses money if it lies or sleeps.
mechanics: On Ethereum, a validator is activated by depositing 32 ETH into the deposit contract and running execution, consensus and validator clients. Each 12-second slot one validator is chosen to propose a block and committees attest; attesting and proposing correctly yields ETH rewards, while being offline leaks stake and equivocation is slashed.
failure_modes: Correlated misbehavior (mass slashing) can destroy large fractions of stake; client monoculture means a bug in a majority client can cause correlated penalties across the network; key compromise lets an attacker get the validator slashed.
misconceptions: Running a validator is not passive income — it requires uptime and correct signing, and offline validators steadily lose ETH. Staking through a pool still carries the underlying validator risks.
example: A validator that stays online and attests correctly earns roughly a few percent APR on its 32 ETH; one that is slashed in an isolated incident loses about 1 ETH immediately plus additional penalties over a 36-day forced exit.

name: Miner
definition: A miner is a network participant in a proof-of-work blockchain that expends computation to find valid block hashes, collecting new coins (block subsidy) and transaction fees in exchange for extending the chain.
intuition: Miners are the bookkeepers of a PoW chain who pay for their write access with electricity instead of collateral.
mechanics: Miners gather transactions into a candidate block and repeatedly hash its header with varying nonces until the hash meets the difficulty target; the first to succeed broadcasts the block and earns the block reward (new issuance plus fees). Difficulty retargets so that, regardless of total hash rate, blocks arrive at a target interval.
failure_modes: Miners controlling a majority of hash rate can censor transactions or execute double-spends; falling coin price with fixed energy costs can force miners offline (miner capitulation), temporarily reducing network security.
misconceptions: Miners do not 'create bitcoins out of nothing' — issuance follows the protocol's fixed schedule, and mining revenue competes away toward energy costs. Mining does not verify your personal transactions faster; it secures the whole chain probabilistically.
example: A Bitcoin miner that finds a valid block currently earns the block subsidy (3.125 BTC after the 2024 halving) plus the fees of all included transactions, roughly every 10 minutes on average across the network.

name: Node
definition: A node is any computer running blockchain client software that connects to peers, propagates transactions and blocks, and verifies data against the protocol's consensus rules.
intuition: Every node keeps its own copy of the ledger and checks the math itself — 'don't trust, verify'.
mechanics: Full nodes download and validate every block and re-execute transactions, pruning old state; archive nodes additionally retain all historical states; light nodes download only block headers and request proofs from full nodes. On Ethereum a node pairs an execution client (EVM/state) with a consensus client (proof-of-stake).
failure_modes: If most users rely on a few hosted node/RPC providers, the network re-centralizes in practice even with many independent nodes; a bug in a dominant client can take down a large share of the network simultaneously.
misconceptions: Running a node does not by itself earn rewards — only miners (PoW) or validators (PoS) are paid. A light node trusts block headers and does not fully verify state.
example: An Ethereum full node stores recent state (typically the last 128 blocks), verifies every new block against consensus rules, and serves data to light clients and wallets via its RPC endpoint.

name: Wallet
definition: A wallet is an application or device that manages a user's cryptographic keys and uses them to view balances, sign transactions and interact with blockchain applications; the assets themselves live on the ledger, not inside the wallet.
intuition: A wallet is a keychain plus a window into the blockchain, not a purse that 'holds' coins.
mechanics: Wallets generate and store private keys (often derived from a seed phrase), derive public addresses, and sign transaction requests that are then broadcast to the network. They come as browser extensions, mobile or desktop apps, or hardware devices that keep keys offline; custodial 'wallets' at exchanges instead entrust keys to the platform.
failure_modes: Phishing sites and malicious approvals trick users into signing transactions that drain their accounts; lost keys or seed phrases mean permanent, unrecoverable loss since there is no password reset.
misconceptions: Coins are not stored 'in' the wallet — only the keys are; switching wallet apps does not move funds. A custodial exchange balance is an IOU, not self-custody of the underlying asset.
example: You open MetaMask, which derives your address 0x5e97...a120 from your private key; when you send 0.5 ETH, the wallet signs the transaction with that key and broadcasts it, and the ledger — not the wallet — records the new balance.

name: Private key
definition: A private key is a secret 256-bit number that controls an externally owned blockchain account: whoever knows it can sign transactions and spend the account's funds, so it must never be revealed.
intuition: The private key is the one true password to your coins — there is no recovery desk if it leaks or is lost.
mechanics: Wallets generate a random private key (64 hex characters); the corresponding public key is derived via elliptic-curve multiplication (ECDSA/secp256k1 on Ethereum), and the address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key. Signing a transaction with the private key proves authorization without revealing the key.
formula: public_key = private_key × G (elliptic curve point multiplication with generator G); address = last 20 bytes of Keccak256(public_key).
failure_modes: Key theft (malware, phishing, insecure backups) gives irreversible control of funds; key loss is final because no one can regenerate a private key from an address — the derivation is one-way.
misconceptions: A private key cannot be recovered from the public address — reversing the hash or the elliptic-curve multiplication is computationally infeasible. Changing a wallet password does not change or protect an already-leaked key.
example: A private key looks like ffffffff...415f (64 hex chars); exposing it once in a screenshot or cloud note lets anyone sweep the account's entire balance in a single signed transaction.

name: Public key
definition: A public key is the openly shareable half of an account's cryptographic key pair, derived one-way from the private key and used by the network to verify signatures and derive the account address.
intuition: It is like your email address for money: anyone can know it and send you funds, but only the matching private key can spend them.
mechanics: The public key is computed from the private key by elliptic-curve multiplication, which is infeasible to reverse. On Ethereum, the account address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key; when a signed transaction is broadcast, nodes recover the public key from the signature to prove the sender's identity.
formula: public_key = private_key × G (one-way elliptic curve multiplication); address = last 20 bytes of Keccak256(public_key), prefixed with 0x.
failure_modes: Sharing a public key or address is safe for receiving funds, but address reuse and public on-chain history destroy privacy since anyone can trace all associated activity.
misconceptions: A public key is not the same as an address — the address is a hash of the public key, and the public key itself is only revealed on-chain when the account first sends a transaction.
example: An Ethereum address such as 0x5e97870f263700f46aa00d967821199b9bc5a120 is derived by hashing the account's public key; anyone can verify that a transaction signed by the matching private key genuinely came from that account.

name: Seed phrase
definition: A seed phrase (recovery phrase) is a human-readable list of typically 12 or 24 words that encodes the entropy from which all of a wallet's private keys are deterministically derived, serving as the master backup for the wallet.
intuition: It is the master key written in words: anyone who reads it owns everything the wallet controls, forever.
mechanics: Wallets following standards such as BIP-39 generate the phrase from random entropy and derive the entire key hierarchy from it, so re-entering the phrase on any compatible wallet regenerates the same accounts. Wallet providers instruct users to write it down offline because it is the only recovery path.
failure_modes: Phishing attacks that ask users to 'verify' their seed phrase are the dominant wallet-drain vector; storing it in cloud notes, photos or email makes remote theft trivial, and losing it makes funds unrecoverable.
misconceptions: A seed phrase cannot be changed after the fact — if it leaks, the only remedy is moving funds to accounts derived from a new phrase. The wallet app's password does not protect a leaked phrase.
example: A 12-word phrase like 'there aeroplane curve vent formation doge possible product distinct under spirit lamp' can regenerate every account in the wallet on a new device; whoever types it into any wallet software gains full control of the funds.

name: Smart contract
definition: A smart contract is a program deployed to a blockchain — a collection of code (functions) and data (state) at a specific address — that executes automatically and exactly as written when called by a transaction.
intuition: A vending machine for logic: given the right inputs and fee, a guaranteed, unstoppable output, with no operator able to intervene.
mechanics: Developers compile code (e.g. Solidity) to EVM bytecode and deploy it via a transaction; the contract then exists as an account type with a balance and storage but no private key. Users and other contracts invoke its functions by sending transactions that pay gas; execution is deterministic and replicated by every node, and deployed code cannot be altered by default.
failure_modes: Bugs are immutable — exploits like re-entrancy or logic errors can drain contracts with no way to patch or reverse; contracts cannot fetch off-chain data themselves and inherit the risks of whatever oracle they trust.
misconceptions: Smart contracts are neither 'smart' nor legal contracts — they only execute code, cannot interpret intent, and cannot access real-world data without an oracle. 'Code is law' fails badly when the code has bugs.
example: A simple contract might hold 100 cupcake balances and release one to any caller who sends 1 ETH; once deployed, no one — including its creator — can change the 1 ETH price or freeze the cupcakes.

name: Gas fee
definition: A gas fee is the payment, denominated in the chain's native currency, that compensates the network for the computational resources a transaction consumes, priced per unit of 'gas' — the protocol's measure of computational effort.
intuition: Gas is the meter on the world's shared computer: every operation you run ticks up a bill you must pay, whether or not the transaction succeeds.
mechanics: Fee = gas units used × (base fee + priority fee). The base fee is set by the protocol per block (adjusting up to ±12.5% based on demand against a target block size) and is burned; the priority fee (tip) goes to the validator to incentivize inclusion. Users can cap total spend with maxFeePerGas, and unused gas is refunded.
formula: gas fee = gas_used × (base_fee + priority_fee); e.g. 21,000 × (10 + 2) gwei = 252,000 gwei = 0.000252 ETH.
failure_modes: Demand spikes can push fees above the value of small transactions, pricing users out; setting a gas limit too low causes the transaction to run out of gas, fail, and still consume the fee.
misconceptions: Gas fees are not paid to a company — the base fee is burned and only the tip reaches the validator. A failed transaction still costs gas because computation was performed.
example: Sending 1 ETH with a base fee of 10 gwei and a 2 gwei tip costs 21,000 × 12 gwei = 0.000252 ETH; the sender pays 1.000252 ETH total, the base fee of 0.00021 ETH is burned, and the validator keeps the 0.000042 ETH tip.

name: Block space
definition: Block space is the finite capacity of each block to include transactions, measured in gas (Ethereum) or bytes/weight (Bitcoin); it is the scarce resource that gas markets price.
intuition: Each block is a truck with a fixed cargo hold leaving at fixed intervals — when more freight shows up than fits, shippers bid up the price of space.
mechanics: Ethereum blocks target half the block gas limit (e.g. 15M of a 30M limit) and can expand to the limit under demand; the base fee rises or falls up to 12.5% per block to push usage back toward the target. Because each transaction consumes gas against this cap, demand for block space directly sets fee levels.
failure_modes: Sustained congestion makes the chain unusable for low-value transactions and invites MEV bidding wars; raising the block limit trades decentralization for capacity by increasing node hardware requirements.
misconceptions: Block space scarcity is a design choice, not an accident — unbounded blocks would centralize validation. High fees signal demand for space, not a broken fee mechanism.
example: If an NFT mint fills blocks to the 30M gas limit for several blocks in a row, the base fee compounds upward by 12.5% per full block, and a simple transfer that cost 10 gwei can jump past 200 gwei within minutes.

name: Mempool
definition: The mempool (memory pool) is each node's local holding area for valid broadcast transactions that have not yet been included in a block; block producers select transactions from it, typically by fee offered.
intuition: It is the public waiting room for transactions — and because everyone can read it, predators can see your trade before it executes.
mechanics: When a user broadcasts a transaction, each receiving node validates it, adds it to its local mempool and gossips it to peers. Validators pick transactions (usually highest priority fee first) when building a block; transactions can linger, be replaced by higher-fee versions, or be dropped. Public visibility of pending transactions enables front-running and sandwich attacks.
failure_modes: Public mempool visibility lets searchers front-run or sandwich pending trades; congestion can leave low-fee transactions pending indefinitely, and private relay channels used to avoid this reintroduce centralization.
misconceptions: The mempool is not a single global queue — each node has its own mempool and they can differ. Inclusion is not FIFO; ordering is at the block builder's discretion and usually fee-driven.
example: A 100 ETH Uniswap buy sits in the mempool for ~12 seconds before inclusion; a sandwich bot sees it, buys the same token in front of it, lets the victim's trade push the price up, and sells immediately after for a profit.

name: Transaction finality
definition: Transaction finality is the point at which a transaction's inclusion in the chain becomes irreversible — on proof-of-stake Ethereum, when the block containing it sits under checkpoints justified and finalized by ≥2/3 of staked ETH, so reversal would require burning at least one-third of all stake.
intuition: Finality is when 'pending' becomes 'set in stone' — before it, the chain can still be rewritten; after it, reversal would cost attackers billions.
mechanics: Ethereum divides time into 32-slot epochs; validators vote on checkpoint pairs, and a checkpoint with a two-thirds supermajority becomes justified, then finalized when the next checkpoint is justified (~2 epochs, ≈13 minutes). In proof-of-work chains finality is only probabilistic: confidence grows with each confirmation but never becomes absolute.
failure_modes: If >1/3 of stake goes offline or votes against finality, the chain stalls and the inactivity leak must burn dissenting stake to recover; bridges and exchanges that credit deposits before finality are exposed to reorg double-spends.
misconceptions: One confirmation is not finality — recent blocks can be reorganized. PoS finality is economic, not absolute: reversal is possible in principle if attackers are willing to be mass-slashed.
example: An exchange crediting ETH deposits waits for finalization (~15 minutes): reverting a finalized deposit would require an attacker to get at least one-third of all staked ETH destroyed, an economically irrational cost.

name: Confirmation
definition: A confirmation is the inclusion of a transaction in a mined/validated block; each additional block built on top counts as another confirmation and exponentially reduces the probability that the transaction is reversed.
intuition: Each confirmation is another layer of concrete poured over your transaction — one layer can be broken through, six is conventional vault-grade.
mechanics: In proof-of-work chains, the probability that an attacker catches up to the honest chain decays exponentially with the number of confirmations (Nakamoto's analysis), so receivers wait for N blocks (conventionally 6 for Bitcoin, ≈60 minutes) before treating payment as safe. On proof-of-stake Ethereum, confirmations culminate in explicit finality after two epochs.
failure_modes: Accepting zero-confirmation transactions exposes the receiver to double-spends; during chain reorganizations, even confirmed transactions can temporarily be dropped back to pending.
misconceptions: 'Confirmed' does not mean 'irreversible' on PoW chains — it is a confidence gradient, which is why high-value transfers wait for more confirmations. The 6-block rule is a convention, not a protocol guarantee.
example: A merchant accepting a $50,000 BTC payment waits for 6 confirmations (~1 hour) because reversing 6 blocks would require an attacker to privately out-mine the honest network for an hour, an astronomically unlikely feat at honest-majority hash rate.

name: Layer 1
definition: A layer 1 (L1) is the base blockchain network itself — such as Ethereum or Bitcoin — that provides its own consensus, data availability and settlement, and on which layer-2 systems anchor their security.
intuition: The L1 is the bedrock courthouse of record: slower and expensive, but its rulings are final and everything built above ultimately defers to it.
mechanics: L1s execute and validate all transactions directly on the base chain, so throughput is bounded by what ordinary nodes can process; scaling the L1 itself (onchain scaling) requires protocol changes. Layer-2 rollups move execution off the L1 but post transaction data or proofs back to it, inheriting its security and finality.
failure_modes: L1 congestion prices out users and pushes activity to less secure venues; a consensus failure or successful attack on the L1 undermines every layer 2 anchored to it.
misconceptions: Not every chain with cheap fees is 'just an L2' — sidechains with their own consensus are separate L1-style systems that do not inherit Ethereum's security. L1 scaling by simply raising block size sacrifices decentralization.
example: Ethereum Mainnet is the L1 that processes ~15M gas of target block usage per 12-second slot; Arbitrum posts its transaction batches to Ethereum so that, even if Arbitrum's operator vanishes, users can reconstruct state and exit via the L1.

name: Layer 2
definition: A layer 2 (L2) is a protocol built on top of a layer-1 blockchain that handles transactions off the base chain to increase speed and throughput while deriving its security from the L1's consensus — chiefly via rollups, state channels, or related constructions.
intuition: An L2 is an express lane that does the fast driving elsewhere but files the paperwork at the L1 courthouse, so the L1's security still backs every transaction.
mechanics: Users transact on the L2 (usually via an operator called a sequencer); the L2 batches transactions and posts compressed data and/or proofs to L1 contracts. Rollups (optimistic or zero-knowledge) anchor data availability and dispute resolution on the L1; true L2s can be exited trustlessly using the on-chain data, unlike sidechains.
failure_modes: Most L2s run a single centralized sequencer that can censor or reorder transactions and is a liveness single point of failure; bridge contracts holding L1 escrow are high-value exploit targets.
misconceptions: Not everything marketed as L2 inherits L1 security — sidechains and validiums secure their own data and are weaker. Cheap L2 fees do not mean the L2 is trustless; sequencer centralization is the norm today.
example: On Arbitrum (an optimistic rollup), a token swap costs a few cents instead of several dollars on Ethereum; the batch containing it is posted to Ethereum, and withdrawals to L1 finalize after a ~7-day challenge window unless a fast-exit liquidity provider is used.

name: Rollup
definition: A rollup is a layer-2 scaling solution that executes transactions off the layer-1 chain and then posts the transaction data (and a state commitment) back to the L1, so that the L1's consensus secures and finalizes the rolled-up state.
intuition: A rollup runs thousands of transactions on a fast side system, then drops one summarized receipt onto Ethereum — the L1 keeps the evidence needed to check or reconstruct everything.
mechanics: An operator batches offchain transactions, executes them, and publishes compressed data (as calldata or blobs) plus a new state root to an L1 rollup contract. Optimistic rollups assume validity and allow fraud challenges; zero-knowledge rollups attach a validity proof. Because the data lives on L1, anyone can reconstruct the rollup state and force exits.
failure_modes: Centralized sequencers can censor or reorder transactions; if data posting stops or the prover/fraud-proof system fails, users may be unable to exit; upgrade keys and admin controls on rollup contracts introduce trust assumptions.
misconceptions: Posting data to L1 does not mean the L1 re-executes the transactions — execution happens offchain and the L1 stores evidence. Rollup transactions are not 'instantly final' — they finalize only when the L1 accepts the batch (and, for optimistic rollups, the challenge window closes).
example: An Ethereum block targeting 15M gas can carry roughly 78,000 compressed rollup transactions per block in theory; a rollup batching 2,000 transfers per post gives users cent-level fees while Ethereum's validators secure the data.

name: Optimistic rollup
definition: An optimistic rollup is a layer-2 rollup that assumes offchain transaction batches are valid by default and relies on a fraud-proof scheme: anyone can challenge a posted state transition during a challenge period, and proven fraud reverts the batch and slashes the operator's bond.
intuition: It is an honor system with a bounty: transactions are accepted unless someone can prove cheating within a week, and the cheater's deposit pays for the mistake.
mechanics: A sequencer batches transactions, posts them to Ethereum (calldata/blobs) with a new state root, and a challenge window (typically ~7 days) opens. Challengers re-execute the disputed step via an interactive bisection protocol settled by an L1 verifier contract; a successful fraud proof rolls back the invalid state and slashes the operator. Withdrawals to L1 must wait out the challenge period.
failure_modes: Security rests on at least one honest watcher submitting fraud proofs — if all watchers fail or are censored, a malicious operator can steal funds; the 7-day withdrawal delay harms UX and pushes users toward trusted fast-exit bridges; centralized sequencers can censor.
misconceptions: Optimistic rollups are not 'less secure versions of Ethereum' in the fraud-proof model — one honest node suffices to defend correct state — but most deployments still have training wheels (upgradeable contracts, permissioned provers). 'Optimistic' refers to the validity assumption, not speed.
example: A user withdrawing 5 ETH from Arbitrum to Ethereum initiates the exit on L2, waits the ~7-day challenge period, then finalizes on L1; alternatively a liquidity provider fronts the 5 ETH immediately on L1 for a fee.

name: Zero-knowledge rollup
definition: A zero-knowledge rollup (ZK-rollup) is a layer-2 rollup that executes transactions offchain and submits a succinct cryptographic validity proof (ZK-SNARK or ZK-STARK) to the layer-1 contract, which verifies the proof and finalizes the new state without re-executing the transactions.
intuition: Instead of 'trust me, challenge me if I cheat' (optimistic), a ZK-rollup posts mathematical proof that every transaction in the batch was executed correctly — verified on L1 in one step.
mechanics: The operator batches transactions, computes new state roots and generates a validity proof attesting that the state transition followed the rules; the L1 verifier contract checks the proof and updates the canonical state root. Because validity is proven up front, withdrawals finalize as soon as the proof is verified, with no challenge period; transaction data is still posted as calldata for reconstructibility.
failure_modes: Proof generation is computationally expensive and often centralized, and proving systems with trusted setups (many SNARKs) break if the setup's 'toxic waste' leaks; bugs in the circuit or verifier contract can silently accept invalid state transitions.
misconceptions: ZK-rollups do not inherently provide privacy — 'zero-knowledge' here proves correctness of computation, and most ZK-rollups publish full transaction data. They are not automatically EVM-compatible; general-purpose zkEVMs are much harder than simple payment circuits.
example: On zkSync Era, a batch of transfers is finalized on Ethereum minutes after the operator submits its validity proof, whereas the same withdrawal on an optimistic rollup would sit in a 7-day challenge window.

name: Bridge
definition: A blockchain bridge is a mechanism that transfers assets, messages or arbitrary data between otherwise isolated blockchain networks, typically by locking or burning assets on the source chain and minting a representation on the destination chain.
intuition: Bridges are ferries between islands that cannot naturally talk to each other — but the ferry company is often the weakest security link in the whole trip.
mechanics: Common designs are lock-and-mint (escrow asset on chain A, mint wrapped asset on chain B), burn-and-mint, and liquidity-network atomic swaps. Trustless bridges rely on the connected chains' own validation (light clients, fraud/validity proofs); trusted bridges introduce external validator sets, multisigs or oracles that users must trust not to collude.
failure_modes: Bridges account for the largest DeFi hacks: smart contract flaws (e.g. the Wormhole exploit), validator collusion in trusted designs, and depegged wrapped assets can all make bridged tokens unbacked; systemic risk compounds because wrapped assets are used as collateral elsewhere.
misconceptions: A wrapped token on another chain is not the same asset — it is an IOU backed by the bridge's custody. 'Trustless' bridges still carry smart contract risk, and native (canonical) L2 bridges are far safer than third-party multisig bridges.
example: To move ETH to Arbitrum via its native bridge, you deposit ETH into the L1 bridge contract and an equivalent amount is credited on L2; using a third-party multisig bridge instead means trusting that a small validator set will not collude to steal the escrow.

name: Oracle
definition: A blockchain oracle is a service that sources, verifies and transmits off-chain data (prices, events, computation results) onto the blockchain so that smart contracts — which cannot access external data themselves — can act on it.
intuition: Contracts are sealed in a deterministic box and can't browse the internet; the oracle is the courier that slips verified notes under the door.
mechanics: An on-chain oracle contract receives data requests; off-chain oracle nodes query APIs or data sources, reach agreement (e.g. via median aggregation across many nodes, as in Chainlink price feeds), and post the result on-chain where any contract can read it. Decentralized oracle networks use multiple independent nodes and sources plus staking/reputation to resist manipulation.
failure_modes: If the oracle reports a wrong or stale price, lending protocols liquidate solvent users or let attackers drain pools with mispriced collateral; single-source or centralized oracles are one hack or outage away from corrupting every dependent contract ('the oracle problem').
misconceptions: Oracles do not make off-chain data trustless — they shift trust to the oracle network's aggregation and incentives. A decentralized oracle with many nodes but one upstream data source still has a single point of failure.
example: Aave reads a Chainlink ETH/USD price feed to value collateral; if the feed briefly reported ETH at half its true price, thousands of loans would instantly fall below their liquidation thresholds through no fault of borrowers.

name: Decentralized exchange
definition: A decentralized exchange (DEX) is a trading venue implemented as smart contracts — usually an automated market maker — that lets users swap tokens directly from their own wallets without depositing funds with an intermediary.
intuition: A DEX is a currency-exchange kiosk run by code: open 24/7 to anyone, and your money never leaves your pocket until the exact moment of the swap.
mechanics: Traders interact directly with on-chain liquidity pools (e.g. Uniswap) whose smart contracts price and settle swaps atomically in a single transaction; liquidity is supplied by other users earning fees. DEXs are permissionless — anyone can trade, provide liquidity, or list a market — and non-custodial, unlike order-book venues that hold user deposits.
failure_modes: Public mempool exposure invites sandwich attacks and worse execution than quoted; shallow pools give huge price impact; unaudited or malicious token contracts and rug-pull pools are common because listing is permissionless.
misconceptions: DEX prices are not set by an order book of other people's bids/asks (in AMM designs) but by pool ratios, and they track external markets only through arbitrageurs. 'Decentralized' does not mean risk-free — smart contract exploits and MEV are native hazards.
example: Swapping 1 ETH for USDC on Uniswap executes entirely within one Ethereum transaction against the ETH/USDC pool: you sign the swap, the pool contract computes the output via x·y=k, and the USDC lands directly in your wallet.

name: Centralized exchange
definition: A centralized exchange (CEX) is a trading platform operated by a company that takes custody of user deposits, runs an off-chain central limit order book to match buyers and sellers, and settles trades on its internal ledger.
intuition: A CEX is a bank crossed with a stock exchange: fast and familiar, but you are trusting the operator with your money the whole time.
mechanics: Users deposit crypto or fiat into exchange-controlled wallets; the exchange matches orders in its own matching engine and updates internal balances, only touching the blockchain on deposits and withdrawals. Most run central limit order books with permissioned access (KYC), and many offer margin, futures and staking services on the same custodial rails.
failure_modes: Custodial risk dominates: hacks, insolvency or fraud (e.g. FTX) can wipe out deposited balances that are only IOUs on the exchange's ledger; withdrawal freezes, opaque rehypothecation and single-venue price manipulation are structural hazards.
misconceptions: Trades on a CEX are not blockchain transactions — they are database entries, which is why they are instant and cheap but also why proof-of-reserves matters. 'Your' balance on a CEX is a claim on the exchange, not on-chain ownership.
example: Depositing 2 BTC to Binance and selling it updates only Binance's internal ledger; the on-chain BTC stays in Binance's omnibus wallet until you withdraw, so if the exchange freezes withdrawals your claim is stuck with it.

name: Automated market maker
definition: An automated market maker (AMM) is a decentralized exchange design that replaces the order book with smart-contract liquidity pools: traders swap against pooled reserves and prices are set algorithmically by a pricing function of those reserves.
intuition: Instead of matching your buy order with someone's sell order, the AMM is a robot counterparty that always quotes a price from the contents of its vault.
mechanics: Liquidity providers deposit token pairs into a pool contract; each swap trades against the reserves and moves the price according to the pool's invariant (e.g. the constant-product rule x·y=k in Uniswap v2). Arbitrageurs align pool prices with external markets, and LPs earn a fee on each swap proportional to their share of the pool.
failure_modes: AMM prices only track external markets through arbitrage, so thin or manipulated pools can trade far from fair value; LPs bear impermanent loss and toxic-flow losses that can exceed fee income.
misconceptions: AMMs do not 'discover' prices independently — they follow prices set elsewhere via arbitrage. Providing liquidity is not passive yield; it is an active short-volatility position.
example: In a Uniswap ETH/USDC pool, a trader buying ETH with USDC adds USDC to the pool and removes ETH, automatically raising the pool's ETH price; an arbitrageur then sells ETH back into the pool until its price matches centralized exchanges.

name: Constant-product market maker
definition: A constant-product market maker (CPMM) is the canonical AMM pricing rule in which the product of a pool's two token reserves must remain constant across trades (x·y=k), so the marginal price is the ratio of reserves and each trade moves the price along a hyperbola.
intuition: The pool is a balanced scale: remove some of one token and the other must grow so their product never shrinks — which is why big orders get progressively worse prices.
mechanics: A swap of Δx of token X for token Y must satisfy (x+Δx)(y−Δy)=k (before fees), giving output Δy = y·Δx/(x+Δx). The instantaneous price is y/x, so price impact grows quadratically with trade size relative to depth; a fee (e.g. 0.3% in Uniswap v2) is taken from the input and accrues to LPs, making k grow slightly per trade.
formula: x · y = k, where x, y are token reserves and k is the invariant; output for input Δx: Δy = y·Δx / (x + Δx) (ignoring fees).
failure_modes: The full-range design spreads liquidity from 0 to ∞, so most capital sits unused and large trades suffer severe price impact in thin pools; when one token trends, arbitrage continuously extracts value from LPs (impermanent loss).
misconceptions: The invariant does not keep k exactly constant — fees make k grow, and k changes whenever liquidity is added or removed. x·y=k also does not prevent LPs from losing money to price divergence.
example: A pool holds 10 ETH and 40,000 USDC (k=400,000, price 4,000 USDC/ETH). Buying 1 ETH requires paying 40,000×1/9 ≈ 4,444 USDC — about 11% above the quoted price, illustrating price impact at 10% of pool depth.

name: Concentrated liquidity
definition: Concentrated liquidity is the Uniswap v3/v4 mechanism that lets liquidity providers allocate capital to a custom price range instead of uniformly across all prices, so the same capital provides deeper liquidity (and earns more fees) where trading actually occurs.
intuition: Rather than spreading butter thinly from price 0 to infinity, LPs spread it thickly on the slice of the curve where the market actually trades.
mechanics: Price space is partitioned into discrete ticks (~0.01% apart); an LP position is defined by a lower and upper tick and only earns fees while the current price is inside its range. Within a range the pool behaves like a bounded constant-product curve; when price exits the range, the position holds 100% of the cheaper token and earns nothing until price re-enters.
failure_modes: Out-of-range positions earn zero fees and hold entirely the depreciated asset, amplifying impermanent loss versus full-range liquidity; concentrated positions demand active management, and naive 'set and forget' ranges systematically underperform.
misconceptions: Higher capital efficiency is not free yield — it is higher leverage on the same LP risk, so impermanent loss per unit of capital is larger, not smaller. Concentrated liquidity does not eliminate the constant-product math; it bounds where it applies.
example: On Uniswap v2's DAI/USDC pool, only ~0.5% of capital served trades between $0.99 and $1.01; a v3 LP allocating $10,000 entirely to the 0.99–1.01 range earns the same fees on that volume as roughly $2M of v2-style liquidity.

name: Liquidity pool
definition: A liquidity pool is a smart contract holding reserves of two (or more) tokens that an AMM uses as the counterparty for swaps; traders trade against the pooled reserves and liquidity providers fund them in exchange for a share of fees.
intuition: It is a communal vault of token pairs: everyone chips in inventory, the vault quotes prices from its contents, and depositors split the toll every trader pays.
mechanics: Providers deposit proportional amounts of both tokens and receive pool shares (LP tokens in v2, NFT positions in v3) representing their pro-rata claim on reserves plus accrued fees. Swaps move the reserve ratio, repricing the pair via the pool's invariant (e.g. x·y=k), and a per-swap fee (e.g. 0.3%) accrues to the pool.
failure_modes: Pools for scam or exploited tokens can be drained or become worthless, and permissionless listing means anyone can create deceptive pools; thin pools give extreme slippage and are easy to manipulate for oracle attacks.
misconceptions: Pool depth (TVL) is not a guarantee of fair pricing — prices still track external markets only via arbitrage. Depositing into a pool is not like depositing into a savings account; the asset mix you withdraw is usually different from what you put in.
example: A Uniswap ETH/USDC pool holding 10,000 ETH and 40M USDC lets a trader swap 100,000 USDC for ~24.9 ETH instantly; the 0.3% fee (~300 USDC) stays in the pool, enriching all LP shares.

name: DeFi liquidity provider
definition: A DeFi liquidity provider (LP) is a user who deposits tokens into an AMM liquidity pool (or lending pool) and in return holds a pro-rata claim on the pool's reserves and the fees those reserves generate.
intuition: LPs are the inventory suppliers of on-chain markets: they rent out their tokens to the pool and get paid a cut of every trade — while silently selling winners and buying losers as prices move.
mechanics: In Uniswap v2, depositing equal values of two tokens mints ERC-20 LP tokens tracking the provider's pool share, redeemable for reserves plus fees; in v3, LPs choose price ranges and receive NFT positions. LP returns equal trading fees plus incentive rewards minus impermanent loss from price divergence.
failure_modes: Impermanent loss in trending markets can exceed fee income, leaving LPs worse off than holding; LP positions also inherit smart contract risk, and v3 ranges can drift out-of-range and earn nothing.
misconceptions: LP'ing is not risk-free yield — it is a short-volatility position whose PnL = fees + rewards − impermanent loss. High APRs quoted from incentive tokens usually decay as more liquidity joins and token emissions fall.
example: An LP supplying $5,000 of ETH and $5,000 of USDC to a 0.3%-fee pool with $1M daily volume and $10M TVL earns roughly 0.3%×$1M×(10k/10M) ≈ $3/day before considering impermanent loss.

name: Impermanent loss
definition: Impermanent loss is the difference in value between depositing tokens into an AMM liquidity pool and simply holding those same tokens: as relative prices change, arbitrage rebalances the pool so the LP ends up with less of the appreciating asset and more of the depreciating one.
intuition: The pool automatically sells your winners and buys your losers; if prices snap back the 'loss' vanishes — but if you withdraw while prices have diverged, it becomes real.
mechanics: Under x·y=k, when the external price of one token rises, arbitrageurs buy it from the pool until the internal price matches, changing the reserve ratio. For a relative price change of factor r, IL = 2√r/(1+r) − 1 vs holding (e.g. r=2 → −5.7%, r=5 → −25.5%), independent of direction. Fees and incentives may or may not offset it.
formula: IL(r) = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1, where r is the ratio of the new relative price to the price at deposit.
failure_modes: IL grows non-linearly with divergence, so volatile or trending pairs can leave LPs deep underwater versus holding even after fees; concentrated liquidity amplifies IL per unit of capital when price leaves the range.
misconceptions: 'Impermanent' does not mean harmless — the loss is permanent the moment you withdraw at a diverged price, and the original price often never returns. Fee income is not guaranteed to cover IL; for many pairs and periods it does not.
example: Deposit 1 ETH + 1,000 USDC when ETH = $1,000 (pool: 10 ETH + 10,000 USDC, you own 10%). ETH doubles to $2,000; arbitrage leaves the pool at 7.071 ETH + 14,142 USDC. Your 10% withdrawal is worth $2,828 vs $3,000 for holding — a 5.7% impermanent loss.

name: Slippage tolerance
definition: Slippage tolerance is the maximum deviation a user accepts between the expected price of an on-chain swap and the price it actually executes at; if execution would exceed this bound, the transaction reverts.
intuition: It is the 'don't fill me worse than X' dial on a DEX trade — your insurance against the price moving between signing and execution.
mechanics: Price slippage is the gap between the quoted price when a swap is submitted and the realized execution price, caused by other trades landing first and by the trade's own price impact. Wallets/routers encode slippage tolerance as a minimum output amount; if the pool cannot deliver at least that much, the transaction fails (and only gas is lost).
failure_modes: Setting tolerance too high invites sandwich attackers to push execution to the worst allowed price; too low, and transactions revert repeatedly in volatile markets, wasting gas without executing.
misconceptions: Slippage tolerance does not reduce price impact — it only caps the damage you accept; the trade's own impact is computed by the AMM regardless. A failed, reverted swap still costs gas.
example: Swapping 50,000 USDC for ETH quoted at 12.5 ETH with 0.5% slippage tolerance sets a minimum of 12.4375 ETH; if a sandwich bot moves the pool so you'd only get 12.3 ETH, the transaction reverts instead of filling.

name: Price impact in AMMs
definition: Price impact is the change in a pool's token price caused by a trader's own swap: under the constant-product rule, larger trades relative to pool depth execute at progressively worse prices, and the impact is deterministic given pool reserves.
intuition: It is how much your own order moves the market against you — the bigger the bite you take from the pool, the worse the price of the last bite.
mechanics: In a CPMM, output is Δy = y·Δx/(x+Δx), so average execution price worsens as Δx grows relative to reserve x; price impact ≈ Δx/(x+Δx) for small trades, growing quadratically. Unlike slippage (which includes other trades landing first), price impact is caused solely by your own trade and is shown by DEX interfaces before signing.
formula: For x·y=k, output Δy = y·Δx / (x + Δx); impact ≈ 1 − (execution price / spot price) = Δx / (x + Δx).
failure_modes: In thin pools even modest trades move prices several percent, and a single large swap can be exploited as a temporary oracle price for attacks on dependent protocols; splitting orders reduces but cannot eliminate impact.
misconceptions: Price impact is not a fee — it is an execution cost paid through a worse exchange rate, and it is not the same as slippage, which also includes price movement from other actors before your trade confirms.
example: A pool holds 10 ETH and 40,000 USDC (spot 4,000). A 10,000 USDC buy (25% of USDC depth) returns 2 ETH at an average 5,000 USDC/ETH — a 25% price impact, versus ~0% impact for a tiny trade.

name: Sandwich attack
definition: A sandwich attack is an MEV strategy in which an attacker sees a victim's pending DEX trade in the mempool, inserts a buy immediately before it (front-run) and a sell immediately after it (back-run), profiting from the price movement the victim's own trade creates.
intuition: A predator spots your big market order in the waiting room, jumps the queue to buy ahead of you, lets your purchase push the price up, then dumps on you — you become their exit liquidity.
mechanics: The searcher computes the victim trade's price impact, front-runs with a buy that raises the price, lets the victim's trade execute at a worse rate (bounded only by their slippage tolerance), then back-runs with a sell at the elevated price. The profit comes directly from the victim's worse execution, net of gas and bribes to builders for ordering.
failure_modes: Sandwiches are not atomic, so the attacker bears inventory risk if the back-run fails or another bot interferes (e.g. 'salmonella' counter-attacks); tight victim slippage settings can make the attack unprofitable.
misconceptions: Sandwiching is not hacking the victim's wallet — it exploits the public ordering of otherwise valid transactions. High slippage tolerance is the attacker's margin; private transaction relays mitigate but centralize order flow.
example: A user buys 10,000 UNI with DAI on Uniswap with 5% slippage; a bot front-runs a UNI buy, the user's trade executes near the worst allowed price, and the bot's immediate sell extracts the difference — the user receives materially fewer UNI than quoted.

name: Blockchain front-running
definition: Blockchain front-running is the practice of observing a profitable pending transaction (in the public mempool or via privileged ordering access) and inserting one's own transaction ahead of it to capture the opportunity first.
intuition: It is the on-chain version of a broker trading ahead of a client's order — except the order flow is broadcast publicly to everyone, so bots do it at machine speed.
mechanics: Because pending transactions are visible before inclusion, bots monitor the mempool, simulate transactions, and copy or preempt profitable ones, winning priority through higher gas bids (priority gas auctions) or by paying block builders via private relays (e.g. Flashbots). Generalized front-runners even clone arbitrary profitable transactions with their own address substituted.
failure_modes: Front-running gas auctions historically congested the whole network and raised fees for everyone; extreme incentives to capture large MEV can tempt block producers to reorder or reorg blocks, destabilizing consensus.
misconceptions: Front-running is not unique to insiders — on public chains anyone can do it, which is why it is an arms race won by latency and gas-bidding infrastructure. Using a private relay hides your trade from the public mempool but not from the relay/builder.
example: A bot sees a pending transaction buying a mispriced NFT for 1 ETH worth 5 ETH, resubmits the identical purchase with its own address and a higher gas tip, and wins the listing before the original buyer's transaction executes.

name: Back-running
definition: Back-running is an MEV strategy in which a bot places its transaction immediately after a target transaction in the same block, profiting from the state change the target creates — most commonly arbitraging a price dislocation right after a large trade or an oracle update.
intuition: Instead of jumping the queue, the bot waits for your transaction to move the market, then cleans up the mispricing you left behind in the very same block.
mechanics: Searchers simulate the post-state of pending transactions (e.g. a large DEX swap that unbalances a pool, or a liquidation event) and submit a transaction that must execute directly after — buying the now-cheap asset on one venue and selling on another atomically. Placement is bought via gas bidding or bundle submission to block builders; the second leg of a sandwich attack is a back-run.
failure_modes: Competition is so intense that most profit is bid away to validators as gas/bribes (searchers may pay >90% of MEV revenue in fees); failed back-runs still cost gas, and racing bots can make the trade revert.
misconceptions: Back-running is not parasitic in all cases — DEX arbitrage back-runs are what keep AMM prices aligned with external markets, a service the ecosystem depends on; the harmful variant is when it extracts value from users (e.g. sandwiches).
example: A 1,000 ETH sell on Uniswap pushes ETH's pool price 2% below Binance; a back-running bot buys ETH in the same block right after the sell and offloads it on a centralized exchange, pocketing the spread minus fees.

name: Maximal extractable value
definition: Maximal extractable value (MEV) is the maximum value that can be extracted from block production — beyond the standard block reward and gas fees — by including, excluding, or reordering transactions within a block.
intuition: Whoever decides the order of transactions in a block holds a printing press: they can see the future of the block and sell positions in it.
mechanics: Validators (formerly miners, hence the older term 'miner extractable value') control inclusion and ordering; in practice independent 'searchers' find opportunities — DEX arbitrage, liquidations, sandwich attacks — and capture them via gas bidding or sealed bundles (Flashbots/MEV-Boost), sharing most proceeds with validators through builder auctions (proposer-builder separation).
failure_modes: Unchecked MEV degrades user execution (sandwiches), congests the network via gas auctions, and — when MEV in a block exceeds the block reward — creates incentives for time-bandit reorgs that threaten consensus stability; private order flow and builder concentration centralize the network.
misconceptions: MEV is not inherently theft or purely bad — arbitrage and liquidations keep prices consistent and lending protocols solvent. Nor is it eliminable by protocol upgrades alone; it is an intrinsic property of ordering power, only redistributable or mitigated.
example: A searcher spots ETH/DAI priced differently on Uniswap vs Sushiswap and turns 1,000 ETH into 1,045 ETH in one atomic transaction, paying most of the 45 ETH profit to the validator as a bribe for guaranteed inclusion.

name: Flash loan
definition: A flash loan is an uncollateralized loan that must be borrowed and repaid (plus fee) within a single blockchain transaction; if repayment does not complete, the entire transaction reverts as if the loan never happened.
intuition: It is a loan that exists only for the duration of one atomic operation — millions of dollars, no collateral, but you must hand it back before the transaction closes or everything unwinds.
mechanics: The borrower contract calls the pool (e.g. Aave's flashLoanSimple), receives the funds, executes arbitrary logic (arbitrage, liquidation, collateral swap), and the pool pulls back principal plus fee (~0.05% on Aave) at the end of the same transaction; failure to approve repayment reverts all state changes. Atomicity makes the loan risk-free for the lender.
failure_modes: Flash loans supercharge exploits: attackers borrow huge capital to manipulate thin DEX prices or oracle feeds, drain vulnerable protocols, and repay in the same transaction — the loan is a tool, and most famous 'flash loan attacks' exploited other contracts' logic, not the lender.
misconceptions: Flash loans do not give free money — the borrowed capital must be repaid in the same transaction, so profit must come from a real opportunity executed atomically. The lender is not the party at risk in flash-loan attacks.
example: Borrow 10,000 ETH via Aave flash loan, buy an asset priced at $1.00 on exchange A, sell it at $1.10 on exchange B, repay 10,005 ETH (0.05% fee) — all in one transaction; if any leg fails, the whole transaction reverts and the loan never existed.

name: Lending protocol
definition: A lending protocol is a set of smart contracts (e.g. Aave, Compound) that pools supplied assets and lets borrowers draw loans against deposited collateral, with interest rates, collateral requirements and liquidations enforced automatically by code.
intuition: It is a pawnshop run by a robot: depositors earn interest, borrowers post more collateral than they take, and the robot seizes and sells the collateral the moment the loan turns unsafe.

failure_modes: Oracle failure or manipulation can trigger wrongful liquidations or let attackers borrow against worthless collateral; fast crashes can outrun liquidators and leave the protocol with bad debt; smart contract exploits and governance parameter mistakes are systemic risks.
misconceptions: DeFi lending is not peer-to-peer matching — lenders face the pool, and borrowers face the protocol, with rates set by utilization curves. Deposit insurance does not exist; 'safe' yields embed smart contract, oracle and liquidation risk.
example: A user supplies $10,000 of ETH to Aave (80% liquidation threshold) and borrows $6,000 of a stablecoin; interest accrues to suppliers from the borrower's rate, and if ETH falls enough that the health factor crosses 1, liquidators repay part of the debt and seize discounted ETH.

name: Collateral factor
definition: The collateral factor is the per-asset parameter that determines how much borrowing power a unit of deposited collateral confers, expressed as a percentage of the collateral's value; in Aave V3 this concept is split into LTV (borrowing power for new loans) and liquidation threshold (the undercollateralization trigger).
intuition: It is the haircut the protocol applies to your collateral: $100 of a blue-chip asset might count as $80 of borrowing power, while a volatile token counts as far less.
mechanics: Each listed asset has a governance-set collateral factor/LTV reflecting its volatility and liquidity risk. A user's total borrowing capacity is the sum over collateral assets of value × factor; borrowing beyond it is impossible, and positions drifting past the (higher) liquidation threshold become liquidatable. Riskier or less liquid assets get lower factors.
formula: Borrowing capacity = Σ (collateral_i × price_i × factor_i); e.g. $10,000 ETH at 80% → $8,000 max borrow.
failure_modes: Factors set too high for illiquid collateral let bad debt accumulate because liquidators cannot exit seized collateral profitably; factors changed by governance can shift risk parameters on live positions.
misconceptions: The collateral factor is not the interest rate — it caps loan size, not cost. Depositing more collateral value does not always raise borrowing power proportionally if the asset has a low or zero factor.
example: Aave V3's stablecoin E-Mode category uses 97% LTV and 98% liquidation threshold, while a volatile long-tail asset in isolation mode might carry 50% LTV with a hard debt ceiling.

name: Loan-to-value ratio
definition: Loan-to-value (LTV) is the ratio of the borrowed amount to the value of the collateral securing it; in DeFi lending, each asset's maximum LTV caps how much can be newly borrowed against it.
intuition: LTV is the leverage dial on a collateralized loan: 75% LTV means every $100 of collateral backs at most $75 of new borrowing.
mechanics: In Aave, a user's maximum borrowing power is Σ(collateral value × asset LTV); opening a borrow that would exceed it reverts. LTV is set per asset by governance below the liquidation threshold, leaving a buffer so borrowers are not instantly liquidatable at max borrow; E-Mode categories raise LTV for correlated pairs (e.g. stablecoins at 97%).
formula: LTV = borrow value / collateral value; max borrow = Σ (collateral_i × price_i × LTV_i).
failure_modes: Borrowing at maximum LTV leaves almost no buffer: a small adverse price move or accrued interest pushes the position to liquidation; LTV does not protect against oracle mispricing of the collateral itself.
misconceptions: A higher max LTV is not 'better collateral' in economic terms — it is a risk parameter choice trading capital efficiency against liquidation safety. LTV caps new borrows; the liquidation threshold, a separate higher number, triggers liquidations.
example: With $10,000 of ETH collateral at 75% LTV you can borrow up to $7,500; if ETH's liquidation threshold is 80%, your loan becomes liquidatable only once debt exceeds $8,000 (through price drops or interest).

name: Health factor
definition: The health factor is Aave's numeric measure of how safe a borrow position is: the collateralization of the account weighted by liquidation thresholds, divided by total borrows — a value below 1 means the position can be liquidated.
intuition: It is a fuel gauge for your loan: comfortably above 1 is green, approaching 1 is the warning light, below 1 liquidators take the car.
mechanics: Health factor = (Σ collateral_i in ETH × liquidation threshold_i) / total borrows in ETH. It rises when collateral appreciates or debt is repaid, and falls when collateral drops or debt grows (including accrued interest). Users improve it by supplying more collateral or repaying; liquidators monitor accounts for HF < 1.
formula: HF = (Total collateral value × weighted avg liquidation threshold) / Total borrow value; HF < 1 → liquidatable.
failure_modes: HF depends entirely on oracle prices, so oracle failure or L2 sequencer downtime can make HF misleading exactly when it matters; in violent crashes HF can skip from safe to insolvent before liquidators act, leaving bad debt.
misconceptions: HF = 1 is not where you 'start losing money' — you lose value continuously as collateral falls; HF just marks the point where the protocol allows others to seize it. A high HF today says nothing about HF tomorrow in volatile collateral.
example: Supplying $10,000 of ETH at an 80% liquidation threshold and borrowing $6,000 of GHO gives HF = (10,000×0.8)/6,000 = 1.333; if ETH falls 30%, HF drops to ~0.93 and the position is liquidatable.

name: Liquidation threshold
definition: The liquidation threshold is the per-asset percentage of collateral value at which a borrow position is deemed undercollateralized and becomes eligible for liquidation — effectively the maintenance margin of a DeFi loan.
intuition: It is the tripwire on your collateral: once your debt exceeds this share of what you posted, the protocol declares the loan unsafe and lets liquidators step in.
mechanics: Aave Governance sets a liquidation threshold per asset (e.g. 80% for ETH, 97-98% for stablecoin E-Mode). The account's weighted average threshold enters the health factor formula; when HF falls below 1, a liquidationCall repays up to 50% of debt (100% if deeply insolvent) and seizes collateral at a discount. The threshold sits above LTV, giving borrowers a buffer between max borrow and liquidation.
formula: Position liquidatable when: borrows > Σ(collateral_i × liquidation threshold_i).
failure_modes: Thresholds set too high for volatile assets let insolvency arrive before liquidators can profitably act; governance misconfiguration or oracle errors can liquidate healthy users or fail to liquidate dying ones.
misconceptions: The liquidation threshold is not the same as max LTV — LTV limits new borrowing, the (higher) threshold triggers liquidation; confusing them leads borrowers to think max-borrowed positions are safe. It is a parameter, not a market-derived guarantee.
example: With ETH's 80% threshold, a borrower with $10,000 ETH and $7,900 debt is still safe (HF ≈ 1.013), but a further $150 drop in collateral value or $150 of accrued interest crosses HF < 1 and opens the position to liquidators.

name: Liquidation bonus
definition: The liquidation bonus (or penalty) is the discount at which a liquidator can claim a borrower's collateral when repaying their debt — the economic incentive that makes third-party liquidation profitable.
intuition: It is the bounty for the repo agent: repay part of a failing loan and you get to buy the borrower's collateral at a few percent below market.
mechanics: When HF < 1, anyone can call liquidationCall, repay up to 50% of the debt (100% if HF is below the close-factor threshold), and receive collateral worth debt repaid × (1 + bonus). Bonuses are set per asset by governance (e.g. ~5% on majors, higher on risky assets); the discount is the borrower's liquidation penalty.
formula: Collateral seized = (debt repaid × (1 + liquidation bonus)) / collateral price; e.g. repay $1,000 at 5% bonus → $1,050 of collateral.
failure_modes: Bonuses that are too small fail to attract liquidators in congestion or crashes (bad debt accumulates); too large, and they over-punish borrowers and invite liquidation-hunting manipulation of oracle prices.
misconceptions: The bonus is not free money for liquidators — competition, gas costs and price slippage on seized collateral eat most of it. Borrowers lose the bonus on top of their market losses; it is a penalty, not a fee rebate.
example: A liquidator repays $5,000 of a failing loan backed by ETH at a 5% bonus and receives $5,250 worth of the borrower's ETH, profiting ~$250 minus gas and any slippage when selling the ETH.

name: Overcollateralized loan
definition: An overcollateralized loan is a loan whose collateral value exceeds the borrowed amount — the standard structure of DeFi lending, where borrowers must post more than they take because there is no credit assessment or recourse beyond the collateral.
intuition: Borrow $70 by locking up $100: the lender never checks your credit because your collateral is already worth more than the debt and can be seized instantly.
mechanics: Lending protocols enforce overcollateralization through per-asset LTV caps (e.g. 75-80%) and liquidation thresholds: oracles revalue collateral continuously, and positions drifting toward undercollateralization (health factor < 1) are liquidated permissionlessly to keep the protocol solvent. Interest accrues on the debt, slowly consuming the collateral buffer.
formula: Collateralization ratio = collateral value / borrow value > 1 (e.g. $10,000 collateral / $6,000 debt ≈ 1.67).
failure_modes: Overcollateralization protects only while collateral is liquid and correctly priced: flash crashes, oracle failures or illiquid collateral can flip a loan to undercollateralized before liquidators respond, creating protocol bad debt.
misconceptions: Overcollateralized borrowing is capital-inefficient by design, not a flaw to be fixed by higher LTVs alone — it substitutes collateral for creditworthiness. It also does not make the loan risk-free for the borrower, who can still be liquidated at a penalty.
example: Locking $15,000 of ETH to borrow $7,500 of USDC (50% effective LTV against an 80% threshold) lets you spend dollars without selling ETH, but a ~47% ETH drawdown makes the position liquidatable.

name: Under-collateralized loan
definition: An under-collateralized loan is a loan where the borrower's collateral is worth less than the outstanding debt — either by design (credit-based or flash loans) or by deterioration (a liquidated-too-late position that becomes protocol bad debt).
intuition: It is lending on trust rather than on locked value — normal in banking, but the exception in DeFi, where code cannot chase a borrower for the difference.
mechanics: Mainstream DeFi lending is overcollateralized, so under-collateralized lending appears only in special forms: flash loans (zero collateral, repaid atomically in the same transaction), credit delegation (a depositor delegates borrowing power to a trusted party), and undercollateralized institutional credit pools with legal agreements. When a normal position becomes undercollateralized faster than liquidators act, the deficit becomes bad debt socialized across the protocol.
failure_modes: Without excess collateral, default risk returns: credit delegation and institutional pools depend on legal enforcement or reputation rather than code, and defaults cannot be clawed back trustlessly; bad debt from failed liquidations is absorbed by the protocol's suppliers.
misconceptions: Under-collateralized does not mean unsecured-in-the-moment for flash loans — atomicity is a stronger guarantee than collateral. Conversely, an 'overcollateralized' loan is only as safe as its collateral's liquidity and oracle, and can silently become undercollateralized in a crash.
example: A flash loan of 50,000 ETH is 'undercollateralized' for ~12 seconds yet riskless to Aave because repayment is enforced in the same transaction; by contrast, a $1M institutional credit line with $600k collateral relies on contracts and courts if the borrower defaults.

name: Staking
definition: Staking is the act of depositing a network's native token to activate validator software that secures a proof-of-stake chain — proposing and attesting to blocks — in exchange for protocol rewards, with penalties (slashing) for misbehavior or downtime.
intuition: Staking is posting a performance bond to become part-time infrastructure: do the work honestly and you earn a yield on your deposit; cheat or sleep and part of the deposit burns.
mechanics: On Ethereum, solo staking requires 32 ETH and running execution, consensus and validator clients; rewards accrue for attestations, block proposals and sync duties, while offline validators leak small penalties and equivocating validators are slashed and ejected. Alternatives with lower barriers include pooled staking, staking-as-a-service, liquid staking and exchange staking, each adding its own trust assumptions.
failure_modes: Slashing (including correlated mass slashing) and inactivity penalties reduce stake; custodial and pooled staking concentrate funds and validators, creating central points of failure; staking yields are diluted as more of the supply stakes (issuance per validator falls with total stake).
misconceptions: Staking is not a risk-free interest account — rewards pay for active duties and capital at risk, and third-party staking adds counterparty and smart contract risk. The APR is not fixed: it falls as total stake rises and varies with network activity (tips, MEV).
example: A solo staker with 32 ETH earns roughly 3-4% APR from consensus rewards plus priority fees and MEV when proposing blocks; a validator offline for days loses small daily penalties, while double-signing can cost 1+ ETH and forced exit.

name: Liquid staking token
definition: A liquid staking token (LST) is a transferable token issued by a liquid staking protocol (e.g. Lido's stETH) that represents a claim on staked assets plus accruing rewards, letting stakers stay liquid and use their stake in DeFi while validators do the work.
intuition: It is a receipt for your staked ETH that trades like ETH itself — you earn staking yield while still being able to sell, lend or LP the receipt.
mechanics: Users deposit ETH into the staking pool; the protocol stakes it across a set of professional node operators and mints stETH (or similar) to the depositor. The token's balance or exchange rate grows with staking rewards net of a protocol fee (Lido takes 10% of rewards), and it can be traded, used as collateral, or redeemed for the underlying (subject to withdrawal queues).
formula: User APR ≈ protocol staking APR × (1 − protocol fee); e.g. 3.2% × (1 − 0.10) ≈ 2.9%.
failure_modes: LSTs can trade below their underlying value (depeg) during market stress or withdrawal congestion, and leveraged looping of LST collateral unwinds violently when the peg slips; smart contract bugs, operator slashing and governance capture add layers beyond native staking risk.
misconceptions: An LST is not pegged 1:1 by arbitrage the way a stablecoin is — secondary-market price floats and can deviate for months. 'Liquid' also does not mean instantly redeemable: native withdrawals queue, so liquidity depends on DEX depth.
example: Deposit 10 ETH into Lido and receive ~10 stETH; a year later the position represents ~10.3 ETH of staking rewards, and throughout you could have supplied the stETH as Aave collateral to borrow stablecoins.

name: Restaking
definition: Restaking is the reuse of already-staked ETH or liquid staking tokens as cryptoeconomic security for additional services (Actively/Autonomously Verifiable Services, AVSs), letting those services borrow Ethereum's trust while stakers earn extra rewards and accept extra slashing conditions.
intuition: It is posting the same collateral as bail for multiple jobs at once: more income from one deposit, but any job can trigger forfeiture of the shared stake.
mechanics: On EigenLayer, stakers deposit native ETH or LSTs into restaking contracts and delegate to operators who run AVS software (oracles, bridges, data-availability layers). AVSs pay rewards to operators and stakers for correct service and can slash the restaked stake if commitments are broken — extending Ethereum-grade economic security without each service bootstrapping its own validator set.
failure_modes: Stacked slashing conditions mean a bug or dispute in any single AVS can destroy stake that also secures others; leverage-like recursive restaking (LSTs used as collateral to restake) creates contagion paths where one depeg or slash cascades across services.
misconceptions: Restaking does not create new security from nothing — it re-hypothecates the same stake, so total security is only as strong as the weakest slashing regime in the stack. Extra yield is compensation for extra slashing risk, not free return.
example: A staker restakes 32 ETH worth of stETH on EigenLayer and delegates to an operator serving a data-availability AVS; they earn Ethereum staking rewards plus AVS rewards, but an AVS slashing event can burn the same stake backing both.

name: Yield farming
definition: Yield farming is the practice of deploying crypto assets across DeFi protocols — lending pools, liquidity pools, staking — to maximize returns from interest, trading fees and token incentives, often moving capital frequently to chase the highest rates.
intuition: It is rate-chasing on steroids: farmers shuttle capital to wherever the combination of fees, interest and reward tokens pays the most this week.
mechanics: Farmers supply liquidity or collateral to protocols and harvest multiple income streams: base yield (fees/interest) plus incentive token emissions. Strategies include leveraged looping (deposit, borrow, redeposit) and auto-compounding vaults; net return must be weighed against gas costs, impermanent loss, reward-token price decay and smart contract risk.
formula: Net farm PnL = fees + interest + reward token value − impermanent loss − gas − borrow costs.
failure_modes: Advertised APYs assume reward tokens hold value — emissions-driven yields collapse when the token dumps; unaudited farms are frequent rug/exploit targets, and leveraged loops liquidate catastrophically in drawdowns.
misconceptions: Triple-digit APYs are not sustainable yield — they are mostly marketing paid in inflationary tokens whose sell pressure the farmer joins. 'Auto-compounding' compounds losses just as reliably when the underlying position deteriorates.
example: A farmer deposits stETH as Aave collateral, borrows ETH at 2.5%, swaps to stETH and redeposits, looping to ~3x a 2.9% staking yield — until a stETH depeg forces liquidation of the whole stack.
