name: Liquidity mining
definition: Liquidity mining is a token incentive program in which a protocol distributes its governance tokens to users who provide liquidity (or other desired behavior), subsidizing early liquidity and decentralizing token ownership.
intuition: It is paying suppliers in company stock to stock the shelves: the protocol rents liquidity with newly minted tokens instead of cash.
mechanics: The protocol allocates an emission budget to targeted pools; LPs stake their LP tokens in a mining contract and accrue pro-rata governance token rewards (e.g. Uniswap's 2020 program paid 5M UNI per pool to ETH/USDT, ETH/USDC, ETH/DAI and ETH/WBTC LPs). Rewards are additive to trading fees and typically decline as programs end or more capital joins.
failure_modes: Mercenary capital arrives for emissions and leaves the moment they stop, so TVL and liquidity evaporate post-program; large emissions dilute the token and create persistent sell pressure ('farm and dump').
misconceptions: Liquidity mining rewards are not protocol revenue or profit-sharing — they are dilutive token issuance paying for growth. A high liquidity-mining APR says nothing about the pool's organic fee economics.
example: Uniswap's September 2020 liquidity mining program distributed 83,333 UNI per pool per day across four v2 pools for two months; participating LPs earned UNI on top of the standard 0.3% swap fees.

name: Tokenomics
definition: Tokenomics is the economic design of a crypto token: its supply schedule (issuance, burns, caps), distribution (allocations, vesting, airdrops), utility (fees, governance, staking) and the incentive structures that determine how value and behavior accrue around it.
intuition: It is the monetary policy plus cap table plus business model of a token — the rules that decide who gets tokens, when, and why anyone should hold them.
mechanics: Core levers include fixed vs inflationary supply and emission schedules, allocation splits across community/team/investors with vesting, burn or buyback mechanisms, and utility sinks (fee capture, staking, governance). These parameters are set in the whitepaper or governance and drive circulating supply dynamics, dilution and sell-pressure over time.
failure_modes: Low-float/high-FDV designs with heavy insider allocations create structural overhang: unlocks and emissions overwhelm demand; unsustainable incentive emissions fund short-term growth at the cost of long-term dilution and death spirals.
misconceptions: A capped supply does not guarantee scarcity value — emission timing and insider concentration matter more than the headline cap. Price appreciation is not a tokenomics success metric; design quality shows in distribution fairness and sustainable value accrual.
example: Uniswap's UNI: 1B minted at genesis, 60% to the community, 21.3% to team and 18% to investors on 4-year vesting, 15% retroactively airdropped to users, and a 2% perpetual inflation after year 4 — a complete tokenomic specification in one announcement.

name: Circulating supply
definition: Circulating supply is the number of tokens currently issued and available to the market — excluding locked, vested, escrowed or not-yet-minted tokens — and is the supply basis for the conventional market capitalization.
intuition: It is the float: the tokens that could actually change hands today, not the ones still locked in team vaults or scheduled for future emission.
mechanics: Different providers compute it differently: reported circulating supply is typically sourced from project disclosures (Coin Metrics' 'Estimated Market Cap' uses circulating supply from project/CoinGecko feeds), while on-chain approaches count issued native units (which can include escrow). The number drifts upward as tokens unlock and emissions accrue.
formula: Circulating supply ≈ total issued − locked/vested/escrowed; Market cap = circulating supply × price.
failure_modes: Circulating supply is partly self-reported, so projects can understate locked supply or treasuries, inflating the apparent float; low-float tokens show deceptively small market caps that hide massive future dilution.
misconceptions: Circulating supply is not directly observable from price feeds and methodologies differ across data providers — comparisons must use a consistent source. It also does not equal 'liquid' supply: much of it may be dormant or staked.
example: A token with 100M circulating, 400M vested-locked and 1B max supply trading at $5 shows a $500M market cap but a $5B FDV; holders face 10x potential dilution as unlocks arrive.

name: Total supply
definition: Total supply is the total number of tokens that have been created (minted) so far, minus any that have been verifiably burned — i.e. all tokens in existence whether or not they are circulating.
intuition: It is the full headcount of minted tokens: circulating plus everything still locked in vesting contracts, treasuries and escrow.
mechanics: Total supply = cumulative issuance − cumulative burns; it grows with emissions (block rewards, unlock-related mints) and shrinks with burns (e.g. EIP-1559 base-fee burning on Ethereum). Locked/vested tokens count toward total supply but not circulating supply, so total ≥ circulating at any moment.
formula: Total supply = Σ minted − Σ burned; Circulating supply ≤ Total supply ≤ Maximum supply.
failure_modes: Projects blur total vs circulating to make valuations look smaller or larger as convenient; tokens in 'ecosystem' wallets technically count as total supply while being economically equivalent to insider float.
misconceptions: Total supply is not the cap — for inflationary tokens there is no maximum, and total supply grows indefinitely. A low total supply number means nothing for price without knowing emission rate and burns.
example: Ethereum's total supply equals all ETH ever issued as block rewards minus all ETH burned via base fees since EIP-1559 — fluctuating near ~120M with no maximum cap.

name: Maximum supply
definition: Maximum supply is the hard upper bound on the number of tokens that can ever exist under a protocol's issuance rules, where such a cap exists — most famously Bitcoin's 21 million.
intuition: It is the ceiling written into the monetary constitution: no matter what happens, there will never be more than this many coins.
mechanics: Protocols with capped issuance hard-code an emission schedule that asymptotically approaches the cap (Bitcoin's subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks until issuance rounds to zero, after which only fees reward miners). Many tokens (ETH, most governance tokens with perpetual inflation) have no maximum supply, so the field is undefined for them.
formula: Bitcoin: Max supply = 21,000,000 BTC; subsidy_t = 50 / 2^⌊t/210,000⌋ BTC per block, converging to 0.
failure_modes: The cap is only as credible as the social consensus defending it — a sufficiently dominant coalition could change the code, and the security budget problem (subsidy → 0, fees must replace it) is unresolved for Bitcoin's distant future.
misconceptions: Not all tokens have a maximum supply, and a big cap is not automatically 'bad' — what matters is emission schedule and utility. 'Max supply reached' does not mean all coins are circulating; lost keys permanently shrink effective float below the cap.
example: Bitcoin's max supply is 21M BTC, of which ~19.9M had been mined by 2025; the final satoshis will be issued around the year 2140 as the 33rd halving approaches zero subsidy.

name: Fully diluted valuation
definition: Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is a token's price multiplied by its total (or maximum) supply — the market capitalization the asset would have if every token that can ever exist were already circulating at today's price.
intuition: FDV is the sticker price of the whole company if all shares, including locked insider shares, traded at today's price — often a fantasy number for low-float tokens.
mechanics: FDV = current price × total/max supply, versus market cap = price × circulating supply. Coin Metrics formalizes a related 'Future Market Cap' using known issuance over the next 10 years. A large FDV-to-market-cap gap quantifies overhang from future unlocks and emissions and is a standard dilution-risk gauge.
formula: FDV = price × total (or max) supply; dilution overhang ≈ FDV / market cap.
failure_modes: FDV assumes future tokens would trade at today's price, which is false under emission-driven sell pressure — it overstates achievable value in either direction; comparing FDVs across projects ignores different float, demand and emission profiles.
misconceptions: A high FDV/low float token is not 'cheap' because its market cap looks small — the FDV is the honest size of the claim on future supply. FDV is also not a price target; it is a static dilution snapshot.
example: A new L2 token trades at $2 with 100M circulating (market cap $200M) but 10B total supply: FDV = $20B, a 100x float gap warning that 99% of supply is still locked and coming to market.

name: Market capitalization
definition: Crypto market capitalization is the total USD value of an asset's supply, conventionally computed as current price multiplied by circulating supply (Coin Metrics' on-chain variant uses all issued native units).
intuition: It is the price tag of the entire network at today's price — the standard yardstick for comparing the size of cryptoassets.

name: Token unlock
definition: A token unlock is the scheduled release of previously locked tokens (team, investor, advisor or ecosystem allocations) into transferable circulation under a project's vesting terms — a predictable supply shock that markets typically front-run.
intuition: It is the day the dam gate opens on insider stock: a known date when a tranche of supply becomes sellable for the first time.
mechanics: Vesting contracts release allocations at cliffs and/or linearly per the published schedule; trackers (e.g. Tokenomist, DefiLlama) index these events. Keyrock's analysis of 16,000+ unlocks found ~90% create negative price pressure, with effects starting ~30 days before the event and team unlocks producing the worst drawdowns (~−25% on average).
failure_modes: Unlocks concentrate sell pressure at known dates, inviting front-running and volatility; opaque or renegotiated schedules destroy predictability, and large unlocks into thin markets can trigger cascading drawdowns.
misconceptions: An unlock is not new inflation — it is previously counted total supply becoming liquid, though the price effect can be identical. Not all unlocks dump equally: ecosystem-development unlocks historically showed slightly positive average effects, while team unlocks were the most negative.
example: A token with $200M market cap unlocking $40M (20% of float) for team and seed investors sees price slide weeks ahead of the date as traders position for the predictable supply expansion.

name: Vesting schedule
definition: A vesting schedule is the pre-committed timetable by which locked token allocations (team, investors, advisors) become transferable, typically combining a cliff (no tokens for an initial period) with linear or batched releases thereafter.
intuition: It is a golden-handcuffs calendar: insiders earn their tokens over years instead of getting them on day one, aligning them with the project's survival.
mechanics: Allocations are locked in smart contracts and released per the published schedule — common shapes are a 1-year cliff followed by 2-3 years of linear monthly unlocks, batch unlocks at the cliff, or hybrids (e.g. Solana combined no-cliff linear community release, a 1-year cliff batch unlock for seed/foundation/validators, and 50%-after-9-months-then-monthly for the team).
failure_modes: Heavy cliff unlocks create cliff-edge supply shocks; schedules enforced only by promises (multisig rather than contract) can be renegotiated, and short vesting relative to project maturity leaves insiders liquid before the product proves itself.
misconceptions: Vesting does not eliminate sell pressure, it only delays it — the overhang remains and markets price it in advance. A '4-year vest' with a 1-year cliff still releases a large lump at month 12.
example: Uniswap's UNI allocated 21.266% to team and 18.044% to investors with 4-year vesting; the governance treasury itself vested 40%/30%/20%/10% across years 1-4, with control unlocked after a 30-day grace period.

name: Token burn
definition: A token burn is the permanent, verifiable removal of tokens from supply by sending them to an unspendable destination or destroying them in-protocol, reducing total supply.
intuition: It is shredding banknotes on-chain: the tokens provably cease to exist, making each remaining token a larger share of the whole.
mechanics: Two forms exist: protocol burns, where issuance rules destroy value automatically (Ethereum burns every transaction's base fee via EIP-1559), and discretionary burns, where projects send tokens to the zero address or a burn() function — often funded by buybacks. Burns are public and auditable, unlike token buyback-and-hold programs.
failure_modes: Burns funded by minting elsewhere (burn-and-mint equilibrium optics) can be theatrics that obscure net issuance; discretionary burn announcements are sometimes used to hype price without changing fundamentals, and burned supply is irreversible if later needed for security budgets.
misconceptions: A burn does not automatically raise price — value accrues only if the burn transfers real economic value (e.g. fee burns) rather than just shrinking a number; burning tokens held by the treasury is accounting, not value creation. Ethereum's base-fee burn is not guaranteed to make ETH deflationary — it depends on burn vs issuance.
example: Since EIP-1559, every Ethereum transaction burns its base fee: at a 20 gwei base fee, a 21,000-gas transfer destroys 0.00042 ETH; over high-demand periods this has burned millions of ETH cumulatively, at times exceeding new issuance.

name: Minting
definition: Minting is the creation of new tokens on-chain, increasing total supply — whether as protocol issuance (block rewards to miners/validators) or as application-level token creation by smart contracts.
intuition: It is the printing press of a token economy: new units come into existence by rule, either paying for security or instantiating new assets.
mechanics: At the protocol layer, minting follows the consensus issuance schedule: Bitcoin's coinbase transaction creates new BTC for the block's miner, and Ethereum issues new ETH to validators for proposals and attestations. At the application layer, contracts mint tokens (e.g. LP tokens on deposit, LSTs on staking, NFTs on purchase) according to their code; unbacked or infinite-mint bugs are a classic exploit.
failure_modes: Smart contract minting flaws (infinite mint, unbacked mint) let attackers fabricate supply and drain pools or depeg assets; at the protocol level, minting is inflation that dilutes holders unless offset by demand or burns.
misconceptions: Mining and minting are related but distinct: PoW miners and PoS validators earn newly minted issuance, but 'minting' also covers any contract-created token. Newly minted rewards are not free value — their cost is dilution of all holders.
example: Depositing 5 ETH into Lido mints ~5 stETH to your wallet (application-level mint), while Ethereum's protocol simultaneously mints small new ETH amounts every slot to pay validators (protocol issuance).

name: Emission schedule
definition: An emission schedule is the predetermined rule governing the rate and timing of new token issuance over time — the protocol's monetary policy expressed as supply growth per block, epoch or era.
intuition: It is the central-bank timetable baked into code: exactly how many new tokens are printed, when, and for whom, years into the future.
mechanics: Bitcoin emits a block subsidy that halves every 210,000 blocks (50 → 25 → 12.5 → 3.125 BTC...) toward the 21M cap; Ethereum issues ETH per epoch to validators with rates that fall as total stake rises, net of base-fee burns. Application tokens define their own schedules for incentives and treasury releases. Coin Metrics' future-supply metrics formalize projecting supply from the known schedule.
formula: Bitcoin subsidy = 50 / 2^⌊height/210,000⌋ BTC per block; annualized inflation = issuance per year / current supply.
failure_modes: Declining emissions create a long-run security-budget question (fees must eventually fund security alone); for application tokens, front-loaded emissions fund growth but guarantee heavy early dilution and sell pressure.
misconceptions: A fixed emission schedule makes supply predictable, not price — demand shocks still dominate valuation. 'Deflationary' claims require net issuance (emissions − burns) below zero, not just a burn mechanism.
example: After the April 2024 halving, Bitcoin emits 3.125 BTC per ~10-minute block (~450/day, ~0.8% annualized); UNI instead has a 2% perpetual annual inflation beginning in year 4 after its 1B genesis mint.

name: Airdrop
definition: An airdrop is the free distribution of tokens to a set of wallet addresses, typically to reward past users, bootstrap a community, or decentralize governance ownership, with eligibility usually set by an on-chain snapshot.
intuition: It is a retroactive thank-you payment and marketing campaign in one: wake up, check your wallet, and there are tokens because you used the protocol before a cutoff date.
mechanics: The project snapshots eligible addresses and activity, then makes tokens claimable (users pay gas to claim) or sends them directly. Uniswap's September 2020 UNI airdrop gave 400 UNI to each of 251,534 historical user addresses (10.06% of supply) plus pro-rata allocations to LPs. Airdrops are often paired with vesting for insiders while community allocations vest immediately.
failure_modes: Sybil farmers create thousands of wallets to harvest eligibility, diluting genuine users; unexpected random airdrops are frequently dusting or scam tokens whose approval transactions drain wallets; large immediate floats can crash the token at listing.
misconceptions: Airdrops are not free money in aggregate — their value comes from dilution and future expectations, and 'connect your wallet to claim' sites are the most common phishing lure. Airdropped tokens may be taxable income at receipt in many jurisdictions.
example: In September 2020, every address that had ever called Uniswap v1 or v2 could claim 400 UNI (worth ~$1,200 at launch); even ~12,000 addresses whose transactions had only ever failed were included.

name: Governance token
definition: A governance token is a token whose primary utility is voting power over a protocol's decisions — parameter changes, treasury spending, upgrades — typically exercised through a DAO's proposal-and-vote contracts.
intuition: It is a shareholder ballot in token form: holding it gives you a say in how the protocol runs, weighted by how much you hold.
mechanics: Holders (or their delegates) create and vote on proposals; if quorum and majority thresholds pass, execution happens automatically or via timelocked multisig (e.g. UNI: 1% of supply to propose, 4% quorum, 7-day voting, 2-day timelock). Many governance tokens also carry fee-switch or value-accrual potential, but voting power itself is the core function.
failure_modes: Low participation lets small coalitions or whales capture governance; vote-buying, bribery markets and flash-loan governance attacks can pass malicious proposals; delegation concentrates effective power in a few hands.
misconceptions: A governance token is not equity — it usually grants no legal claim on revenue or assets, only on-chain voting rights. 'Decentralized governance' in practice often means a handful of delegates and a multisig execute most decisions.
example: UNI holders can vote to activate Uniswap's protocol fee switch or spend the community treasury (43% of supply); ENS holders instead delegate their votes to community stewards who vote on their behalf.

name: Protocol revenue
definition: Protocol revenue is the portion of the fees a protocol collects that is kept by the protocol entity itself — flowing to its treasury or governance token holders — as distinct from fees passed through to liquidity providers or other suppliers.
intuition: If fees are the till, protocol revenue is what the house actually keeps after paying the market makers who stocked the shelves.
mechanics: Using DefiLlama's taxonomy: total fees = all value collected from users; revenue = fees kept by the protocol = protocol revenue (to treasury/team) + holders revenue (distributed to token holders via buybacks, burns or dividends); the remainder is supply-side revenue to LPs/lenders. Only the kept fraction represents income attributable to the protocol and its token.
formula: Revenue = ProtocolRevenue + HoldersRevenue; Fees = Revenue + SupplySideRevenue.
failure_modes: Revenue funded by unsustainable incentive cycles or one-off events (liquidation spikes) is not recurring income; comparing revenue across protocols without distinguishing holders vs treasury vs supply-side fractions invites apples-to-oranges valuation errors.
misconceptions: Fees are not revenue — a DEX's 0.3% swap fee mostly belongs to LPs, and only the protocol's cut (if any) is revenue. TVL is not revenue either; it is capital parked, not income earned.
example: If a lending protocol collects $1M of borrower interest in a day and keeps a 10% reserve factor, its daily revenue is $100k — split between treasury accrual and any buybacks for token holders — while $900k is supply-side revenue to lenders.

name: Protocol fees
definition: Protocol fees are all charges and value a protocol collects from its operation — swap fees, borrow interest, liquidation penalties, management fees — excluding the gas costs users pay to the underlying network.
intuition: Fees are the gross till of the protocol: everything users pay in, before it is split between liquidity suppliers, the treasury and token holders.
mechanics: Per DefiLlama's dimensions, dailyFees aggregates all value flows into the protocol's ecosystem (user fees like swap fees and interest, plus yield and staking-derived cuts); it is then decomposed into supply-side revenue (to LPs/lenders), protocol revenue (to treasury) and holders revenue (to token holders). Fee levels and switches are typically set by governance.
failure_modes: Fee revenue can be inflated by circular or incentive-driven volume (wash trading, farm-driven churn) that vanishes when incentives stop; fee-switch promises may never activate, leaving token valuations resting on hypothetical future fees.
misconceptions: Protocol fees are not gas fees — gas goes to the chain's validators, not the application. High gross fees do not imply tokenholder value unless a mechanism routes some share to the treasury or holders.
example: A DEX processing $100M daily volume at a 0.3% swap fee generates $300k daily fees; with no fee switch, 100% is supply-side revenue to LPs and protocol revenue is $0 — flipping the switch might route ~$50k/day to the treasury.

name: Total value locked
definition: Total value locked (TVL) is the aggregate USD value of assets deposited by users into a protocol's own smart contracts — the standard gauge of how much capital a DeFi protocol or chain secures.
intuition: TVL is the size of the vault: how much money users have parked in the protocol's contracts at this moment.
mechanics: Aggregators like DefiLlama sum the value of tokens held in protocol contracts, with filters separating staking (native token), pool2 (LP tokens with the protocol's own token), borrowed deposits and vesting; off-chain assets (e.g. Tether's bank dollars) and native chain staking are excluded. TVL moves with both net deposits and token prices.
failure_modes: TVL can be gamed: recycled/looped deposits, incentive-farmed liquidity with no real users, self-dealt wrapper assets and double-counting across nested protocols inflate it; DefiLlama actively delists such 'unproductive' TVL. It also rises and falls with token prices independent of usage.
misconceptions: TVL is not revenue, profit or even stickiness — mercenary capital can halve it overnight when incentives end. It measures deposited capital, not economic activity; a high-TVL protocol can earn near-zero fees.
example: A lending protocol holding $2B of supplied assets has $2B TVL; if $600M is one whale's deposit earning points with no borrows against it, aggregators may strip it as unproductive, reporting $1.4B of economically real TVL.

name: Stablecoin supply
definition: Stablecoin supply is the total outstanding issuance of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies designed to hold a stable value against a reference asset, usually the US dollar — and is tracked as a proxy for dry powder and fiat liquidity in the crypto economy.
intuition: It is the pile of dollar chips sitting at the crypto casino's tables: when it grows, new fiat-backed buying power is entering; when it shrinks, capital is cashing out.
mechanics: Stablecoins preserve their peg by design: asset-linked issuers (USDT, USDC) back tokens with reserves and mint/redeem against fiat, while crypto-collateralized designs (Dai) mint against overcollateralized vaults and algorithmic ones adjust supply programmatically. Aggregate supply across issuers and chains is observable on-chain and, per FSB/BIS definitions, reflects how much of the ecosystem's settlement happens in dollar terms.
failure_modes: Reserve opacity or a run on an issuer can break the peg (redemptions forcing fire sales of reserve assets); bridge fragmentation splits supply across chains where a wrapped version is only as good as its bridge; regulatory action against a major issuer is systemic for the whole market.
misconceptions: Stablecoin supply growth is not pure bullish flow — some of it rotates from existing crypto sales into stables (risk-off) rather than fresh fiat in. 'Backed 1:1' claims have historically been revised (Tether's composition disclosures), so attestations, not labels, are the evidence.
example: Total stablecoin market value grew from ~$14B in August 2020 to over $300B by 2026, with USDT (~$186B) and USDC (~$79B) comprising roughly 85% of circulation — a scale the BIS flags as a financial-stability consideration.

name: Exchange inflow
definition: Exchange inflow is the volume of coins transferred on-chain into wallets attributed to centralized exchanges over a period, watched as a leading indicator of intent to sell or trade.
intuition: Coins moving onto an exchange are like goods carried into a pawnshop — they are positioned to be sold, even if the sale hasn't happened yet.
mechanics: On-chain analytics firms (Glassnode, CryptoQuant) label exchange-controlled addresses and sum transfers into them; inflow is reported in native units or USD per day. Spikes historically cluster around sharp price moves — the March 2020 crash saw deposit volumes surge as holders rushed to sell — while deposit counts and average deposit size distinguish retail from whale behavior.
failure_modes: Attribution depends on heuristics and labeled wallets, so new exchange addresses or internal reshuffles can masquerade as inflows; inflow ≠ immediate selling, since market makers and custodians also receive deposits for operational reasons.
misconceptions: A large inflow is not a guaranteed dump — coins may sit on the exchange for months, and inflows can also fund derivatives collateral or market-making. Raw inflow without reserve context (is the total balance actually growing?) misleads.
example: During the March 2020 crash, BTC exchange inflow spiked to unusually high volumes as panicked holders deposited to sell; Glassnode noted the number of daily deposits simultaneously hit a 3-year low, meaning the spike was driven by large whale-sized deposits.

name: Exchange outflow
definition: Exchange outflow is the volume of coins withdrawn on-chain from exchange-attributed wallets over a period, commonly read as accumulation or movement to self-custody and reduced immediate sell pressure.
intuition: Coins leaving the exchange are goods carried home from the market — they are being put back into storage rather than offered for sale.
mechanics: Analytics providers sum transfers out of labeled exchange wallets; sustained net outflow shrinks exchange balances (reserves). After the March 2020 crash, outflow declined more slowly than inflow, so net flow stayed negative and the total BTC balance on exchanges dropped ~7% from its February high — a classic accumulation signature.
formula: Net exchange flow = inflow − outflow; negative net flow = reserves shrinking.
failure_modes: Outflows to new exchange wallets or institutional custodians can be misread as self-custody accumulation; reserve decline can also reflect an exchange losing customers (a red flag, not bullishness) — context matters.
misconceptions: Outflow is not proof of buying — coins bought OTC or already held can simply be withdrawn, and a single whale reshuffling custody distorts daily figures. Persistent trends over weeks carry far more signal than one-day spikes.
example: In mid-2020, BTC exchange outflows persistently exceeded inflows at 50-100k BTC per month rates in later Glassnode reporting, draining exchange balances as post-crash accumulators moved coins to cold storage.

name: Exchange reserve
definition: Exchange reserve (exchange balance) is the total amount of a coin held in wallets attributed to centralized exchanges — the immediately sellable inventory sitting on trading venues.
intuition: It is the stock of goods on shop shelves: a bulging shelf means plenty of potential supply for sale; emptying shelves mean holders have taken their coins home.
mechanics: Analytics firms cluster and label exchange addresses and track their aggregate balance over time; reserves fall when outflows exceed inflows (accumulation/cold-storage trend) and rise when inflows dominate (distribution risk). Glassnode documented BTC exchange balances dropping ~7% from their February 2020 high as post-crash withdrawals outpaced deposits.
formula: Exchange reserve_t = Σ balances of labeled exchange addresses; Δreserve ≈ inflow − outflow.
failure_modes: Label coverage is incomplete and changes as exchanges rotate wallets, so levels and trends embed attribution error; reserves also embed coins that will never be sold (market-maker inventory), and reserve trends can invert during exchange insolvencies for non-bullish reasons.
misconceptions: Falling reserves are not mechanically bullish — they can reflect loss of trust in a venue (FTX-style runs) or migration to other custodians. Reserves measure potential, not actual, sell pressure.
example: If labeled exchange wallets hold 2.4M BTC out of ~19.9M supply, roughly 12% of all coins sit as venue inventory; a slide to 2.0M over a year of net outflows signals tightening liquid supply.

name: Realized capitalization
definition: Realized capitalization (realized cap) values each coin at the price when it last moved on-chain, rather than at the current price — approximating the aggregate cost basis of the network and the value 'stored' in the asset.
intuition: Instead of pricing every coin at today's quote, realized cap asks: what did the market actually pay for all these coins when they last changed hands?
mechanics: For UTXO chains, realized cap = Σ (UTXO value × price at the time that UTXO was created); Coin Metrics extends the same idea to account-based chains using each account's last-movement date. Coins last moved cheap are re-priced upward when spent (raising realized cap), and vice versa; lost or ancient coins carry near-zero weight, unlike in market cap.
formula: Realized Cap = Σ value_i × price_last_moved_i (over all UTXOs/accounts).
failure_modes: Exchange internal shuffles and self-transfers re-price coins at current levels without economic change of hands, injecting noise; on account-based chains the 'last moved' convention is cruder than UTXO-level data.
misconceptions: Realized cap is not 'real money invested' — it ignores off-chain purchases and approximates cost basis from on-chain movement only. A coin unmoved since 2009 counts at ~$0, which is a feature (discounts lost coins), not a data bug.
example: Coin Metrics' worked example: accounts holding 100 coins last moved in 2010 ($0), 1,000 coins moved in 2016 ($10) and 500 coins moved in 2019 ($100) give a realized cap of $0 + $10,000 + $50,000 = $60,000 regardless of today's price.

name: Market-value-to-realized-value ratio
definition: MVRV (market-value-to-realized-value) is the ratio of an asset's market capitalization to its realized capitalization, comparing the market's current valuation to the aggregate on-chain cost basis.
intuition: MVRV asks whether holders are, on average, sitting on big paper gains (ratio high, temptation to sell) or paper losses (ratio low, capitulation territory).
mechanics: MVRV = market cap / realized cap. Values >1 mean the average holder is in profit; extremes (>~3.5 historically for BTC) marked late-stage bull markets, while MVRV <1 — price below aggregate cost basis — historically coincided with bear-market bottoms and accumulation zones. It functions as a mean-reversion gauge with realized cap as the mean.
formula: MVRV = Market Cap / Realized Cap.
failure_modes: As market structure matures (ETFs, derivatives, longer holder memory), historical thresholds like 3.5 drift and should not be applied mechanically; exchange-internal coin movements distort realized cap and hence the ratio.
misconceptions: MVRV is not a timing tool for entries and exits — it identifies valuation regimes, and markets can stay 'overvalued' or 'undervalued' for months. It is an analytical framework from on-chain data, not a proven predictive law.
example: With BTC market cap at $1.2T and realized cap at $500B, MVRV = 2.4 — deep aggregate profit historically associated with elevated distribution risk, though below the >3.5 extremes of prior cycle tops.

name: Spent output profit ratio
definition: SOPR (Spent Output Profit Ratio) is the ratio of the fiat value of spent coins at the time they are spent to their value when they were created, measuring whether coins moving on-chain are, on average, being sold at a profit or a loss.
intuition: SOPR is the market's daily P&L receipt: above 1, spenders are cashing out winners; below 1, they are realizing losses.
mechanics: Computed over coins moved in a period: SOPR = Σ(value × price_spent) / Σ(value × price_created) across spent outputs. SOPR >1 signals realized profit-taking (typical in bull rallies), ≈1 is breakeven (often a support/resistance pivot in trends), and <1 marks loss realization or capitulation; aSOPR filters outputs with lifespan under one hour.
formula: SOPR = Σ(value_i × price_spent_i) / Σ(value_i × price_created_i), over outputs spent in the period.
failure_modes: Exchange wallet reshuffles and self-spends register as 'spent' at current price, injecting noise; SOPR describes realized behavior only and ignores the large dormant supply, so it can diverge from aggregate profitability (NUPL/MVRV).
misconceptions: SOPR >1 is not automatically bearish — sustained profit-taking above 1 with quick resets to 1 is the signature of a healthy bull trend; only failure of the 1 level to hold flips the regime. It is a behavioral gauge, not a price predictor.
example: If coins moved today were created at an average $40,000 and are spent at $50,000, daily SOPR = 1.25 — profits being realized; in a correction, SOPR dipping below 1 and then reclaiming it marks seller exhaustion.

name: Net unrealized profit and loss
definition: NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss) measures the network's total paper profit or loss as a share of market cap: the difference between market cap and realized cap, divided by market cap.
intuition: NUPL answers: if every holder sold today, what fraction of the market's value would be profit? It is the aggregate sentiment dial from capitulation to euphoria.
mechanics: NUPL = (Market Cap − Realized Cap) / Market Cap = Relative Unrealized Profit − Relative Unrealized Loss. Above 0 the average holder is in profit; historical sentiment bands are <0 capitulation, 0-0.25 anxiety, 0.25-0.5 hope/optimism, 0.5-0.75 belief, >0.75 euphoria — zones that have bracketed cycle bottoms and tops.
formula: NUPL = (Market Cap − Realized Cap) / Market Cap.
failure_modes: NUPL embeds unrealizable profit of lost coins and long-dormant supply, inflating apparent profit; its historical bands were calibrated on early, smaller markets and drift as the holder base and market structure mature.
misconceptions: NUPL is a macro regime indicator, not a short-term signal — markets can sit in 'euphoria' for months during strong trends and in 'capitulation' through long bear phases. It differs from SOPR, which tracks only coins actually spent.
example: December 2018: NUPL fell to about −0.28 — the average holder underwater by 28% of market cap — coinciding with the $3,200 cycle bottom; April and November 2021 saw NUPL ≈ 0.74-0.75 at the cycle's twin tops.

name: Coin days destroyed
definition: Coin Days Destroyed (CDD) is an on-chain activity metric that weights coin movements by dormancy: each unspent coin accumulates one 'coin day' per day, and spending it destroys those accumulated days, so movements of old coins count far more than churn of young ones.
intuition: Moving 10 BTC held for a decade rings a louder bell than moving 10 BTC bought yesterday — CDD measures the age-weighted significance of what moved.
mechanics: CDD for a spent output = value × lifespan in days; the daily metric sums this over all spent outputs. A 2 BTC UTXO dormant 100 days destroys 200 coin days. Spikes flag long-term holders spending into strength or stress; supply-adjusted CDD normalizes for the steady growth of potential coin days as supply ages and inflates.
formula: CDD = Σ (value_i × lifespan_i [days]) over outputs spent in the period.
failure_modes: Exchange and custodian wallet maintenance periodically destroys huge coin days without any sale, producing false alarms; absolute CDD levels trend upward over the protocol's life, so raw values are not comparable across eras without supply adjustment.
misconceptions: High CDD does not prove old holders are selling — it proves old coins moved, which may be custody reshuffling; context (exchange inflows, SOPR) is needed. Also, repeatedly moving the same coins can destroy at most one coin day per coin per day.
example: Baseline BTC traffic runs under ~5M coin days destroyed daily; readings above 20M days are rare and historically appear during high-volatility episodes when large volumes of old coins move, such as cycle tops or capitulation events.

name: HODL waves
definition: HODL waves are a visualization of the age distribution of the coin supply: colored bands show what fraction of all coins last moved within each age bucket (from <1 day to >10 years), revealing accumulation and distribution cycles.
intuition: It is a geological cross-section of holder behavior: warm young layers swell when coins churn, cool old layers thicken when conviction holders sit tight.
mechanics: Each band's thickness is the share of total supply whose last on-chain movement falls in that age band (bands: <1d, 1d-1w, 1w-1m, 1-3m, 3-6m, 6-12m, 1-2y, 2-3y, 3-5y, 5-7y, 7-10y, >10y). Young bands swell near bull-market tops as old coins are spent and reactivated; old bands thicken in bear markets as accumulation matures into dormancy.
failure_modes: Movement-based aging resets a coin's age even for self-transfers and exchange reshuffles, so apparent 'reactivation' may be pure custody plumbing; bands lag reality by construction — coins must survive to a band's lower bound before appearing in it.
misconceptions: Thickening old bands do not prove accumulation by smart money — they also include lost coins, which grow monotonically and are often assumed out of circulation. HODL waves describe structure, not timing.
example: At bull-market peaks, the <6-month bands have historically swollen toward 50%+ of supply as long-term holders distributed; in deep bear markets, 1y+ bands thicken as coins migrate into cold storage and mature.

name: Hash rate
definition: Hash rate is the estimated total computational power that miners devote to a proof-of-work network, expressed in hashes per second; it is the primary gauge of PoW security expenditure.
intuition: It is the horsepower of the mining fleet: the more hashes per second the network throws at the puzzle, the costlier it is for an attacker to rewrite history.
mechanics: Hash rate is not directly observable on-chain — it is inferred from realized block intervals against current difficulty (Glassnode: average estimated hashes/second produced by miners). Difficulty retargets keep block time constant as hash rate fluctuates, so price-driven miner entry/exit shows up as hash-rate trends with a lag.
formula: Hash rate ≈ difficulty × 2^32 / average block interval (Bitcoin); units: hashes/s (networks now in EH/s).

misconceptions: Higher hash rate does not speed up transactions — difficulty retargets to keep block time constant; it raises attack cost, not throughput. Hash rate also does not measure decentralization: a few pools can control most of it.
example: Bitcoin's mean hash rate reached roughly 1.1 × 10^21 hashes per second (~1,100 EH/s) in recent Glassnode readings; reversing even a few blocks against that wall of computation is economically out of reach for any realistic attacker.

name: Staking ratio
definition: Staking ratio is the percentage of a proof-of-stake network's eligible token supply that is actively staked, indicating how much capital currently secures consensus and how much remains liquid.
intuition: It is the share of the town's wealth posted as security bonds: higher means more skin in the game, but also less free capital circulating in the economy.
mechanics: Computed as staked supply / total (or circulating) supply from on-chain staking data. Per-validator rewards decline as total stake grows (Ethereum's base reward scales with the inverse square root of total staked ETH), so the ratio self-regulates around an equilibrium where marginal yield matches holders' opportunity cost; liquid staking raises the practical ratio by removing the lockup deterrent.

misconceptions: A higher staking ratio is not unambiguously safer — what matters is the distribution of stake across independent operators, not the aggregate. The ratio also does not measure network usage or demand for the token.

name: Funding rate
definition: The funding rate is a periodic payment exchanged directly between long and short holders of a perpetual futures contract, sized by the gap between the perpetual's price and the underlying spot index, designed to pull the perpetual price back toward spot.
intuition: Perpetuals have no expiry to force convergence, so the market rents a tether instead: whoever is on the crowded, premium side pays the other side every few hours.
mechanics: Funding amount = position notional (mark price × size) × funding rate. When the perp trades above spot the rate is positive and longs pay shorts; below spot it is negative and shorts pay longs. On Binance the rate combines a fixed interest component (0.01% per 8h interval by default) with a premium index computed from impact bid/ask prices vs the index, clamped within bounds; only positions open at the funding timestamp pay/receive.
formula: Funding = notional × funding rate; Premium Index = [max(0, impactBid − index) − max(0, index − impactAsk)] / index.
failure_modes: Deeply negative or positive funding in stressed markets makes holding the paying side ruinously expensive, forcing exits that amplify the move; funding is venue-specific, and extreme events can change intervals or caps with little notice.
misconceptions: Funding is not an exchange fee — it is a peer-to-peer transfer (Binance takes no cut), and you only pay or receive it if you hold the position at the exact funding timestamps. Positive funding is not 'free yield' for shorts; it compensates for being on the losing side of crowded positioning.
example: BTC perp at $102,000 vs $100,000 index: positive funding, say 0.01% per 8h — a $1M long pays $100 to shorts each interval (~0.9%/month annualized if persistent), incentivizing shorts and arbitrage that close the premium.

name: Predicted funding rate
definition: The predicted (estimated) funding rate is the exchange's real-time forecast of the funding rate that will apply at the next funding timestamp, computed from the premium index samples collected so far in the current interval.
intuition: It is the meter running on the next funding bill: it shows what longs or shorts would pay if the interval ended right now.
mechanics: Binance continuously samples the premium index (impact bid/ask vs price index, roughly every minute) over the current 8-hour window; the displayed predicted rate is the estimate from samples to date — note the convention that the rate shown at e.g. 09:00 UTC uses the premium dataset from 01:00 to 09:00, not just the final hour. The realized rate is fixed only at the funding timestamp.
formula: Predicted funding ≈ time-weighted average of premium index samples in the current interval + interest component (venue-specific).
failure_modes: The prediction moves with order-book depth: thin or spoofed books late in the interval can swing the final rate away from hours of stable estimates, so positioning on the predicted rate carries estimate risk.
misconceptions: The predicted rate is not locked in — only the rate at the funding timestamp applies, and late premium swings can change it materially. A persistent large prediction is a signal about crowded positioning, not a guaranteed payment.
example: If the premium index has averaged +0.02% through six hours of the interval, the predicted funding shows ~+0.02%+interest; a sharp sell-off in the last hour can drag the realized rate to +0.005% instead.

name: Funding interval
definition: The funding interval is the fixed period between funding payments on a perpetual futures contract — the clock that determines how often the funding rate is applied to open positions.
intuition: It is the billing cycle of the perp tether: every interval, the payment between longs and shorts settles and the meter resets.
mechanics: Binance settles funding every 8 hours at 00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC; only positions open at those timestamps pay or receive (with a ~15-second execution deviation), so closing before the timestamp avoids the charge entirely. In extreme volatility venues can shorten the interval (e.g. to 4h or 1h) to tighten the peg; the default interest component (0.03%/day) is split per interval (0.01% per 8h).
failure_modes: Interval changes during stress (announced per venue rules) alter the carry economics of open positions mid-trade; timing games around timestamps (closing seconds before, reopening after) add noise and can distort the rate's anchoring function.
misconceptions: Intervals are venue- and contract-specific, not universal — assuming 8h everywhere misprices carry; and funding accrues only at the timestamps, not continuously: intraday holding between timestamps costs no funding.
example: A trader opening a BTC long at 08:00:05 UTC still pays the 08:00 funding (within the 15-second deviation window), while one who closed at 07:59 pays nothing regardless of how large the rate is.

name: Perpetual basis
definition: The perpetual basis is the price difference between a perpetual futures contract and the underlying spot (index) price, typically expressed as a percentage; the funding mechanism exists to keep this basis mean-reverting around zero.
intuition: It is how far the tail (perp) wags from the dog (spot): positive when perp buyers pay a premium, negative when perps trade at a discount.
mechanics: Basis = perp price − index price (or (perp/index) − 1). Unlike dated futures, whose basis converges at expiry, perp basis is anchored continuously by funding: a persistent positive basis raises funding, charging longs and attracting cash-and-carry arbitrage (buy spot, short perp, collect funding) that compresses it. Binance's premium index operationalizes the basis using impact bid/ask prices rather than last trade.
formula: Basis % = (perp price / spot index − 1) × 100; annualized carry ≈ average funding rate × 3 × 365 (8h interval).
failure_modes: In liquidation cascades or index outages, the basis can gap violently (perp trading far below spot) before funding arbitrage restores it; basis also embeds the premium index's order-book sampling, so thin books give noisy readings.
misconceptions: A wide positive basis is not a free carry trade — funding can flip or spike, and execution of both legs has costs and margin risk. Perp basis is not a forecast of spot direction; it primarily reflects positioning imbalance.
example: BTC spot index at $100,000 while the perp prints $100,500: basis +0.5%; funding turns positive, and arbitrageurs shorting the perp against spot longs collect ~0.01% per 8h until the premium closes.

name: Liquidation cascade
definition: A liquidation cascade is a self-reinforcing chain of forced position closures: falling prices trigger liquidations whose forced market sells push prices lower still, triggering the next tier of liquidations in rapid succession.
intuition: It is an avalanche on a leveraged mountainside: each margin call knocks loose more snow, and the falling snow triggers the margin calls below.
mechanics: Leveraged positions have liquidation prices set by maintenance margin (or health factors in DeFi); when price crosses a dense cluster of them, engines and liquidators market-sell collateral/positions into the book, deepening the move and hitting the next cluster. Open interest collapses, funding and basis gap, and thin order books amplify each leg — visible in Coin Metrics-style analyses combining OI, funding and liquidation data.
failure_modes: Cascades overshoot any fundamental value — price can wick far below fair levels before recovering (the 'liquidation hunt' zone); exchange risk systems (ADL, insurance funds) socialize residual losses when liquidations cannot fill in time.
misconceptions: Cascades are not proof of manipulation — they are the mechanical consequence of stacked leverage at similar levels, though actors can deliberately push price toward liquidation clusters ('stop hunting'). High leverage in a market is the fuel; any spark works.
example: BTC drops 3% to $97,000 where a dense band of 25x longs liquidates; their forced selling drives $94,000, liquidating 10x longs, then $90,000 — billions in open interest wiped in an hour before buyers absorb the flow.

name: Open interest leverage ratio
definition: The open-interest leverage ratio compares total derivatives open interest to the underlying market's size (spot market cap or exchange reserves), gauging how much leveraged positioning the market carries relative to its real capital base.
intuition: It is the debt-to-equity ratio of the whole market: how big the tower of leveraged bets is compared to the pile of actual coins it leans on.
mechanics: Open interest is the count of outstanding, unsettled derivatives contracts (Coin Metrics collects it per market, ~1-minute cadence, noting venues report one- or two-sided conventions differently). Ratios such as futures OI / market cap or OI / exchange reserve estimate aggregate leverage; elevated readings mean liquidation cascades can move spot violently, and sharp OI drops mark deleveraging events.
formula: OI leverage ratio ≈ futures open interest (USD) / spot market cap (USD) [or / exchange reserve].
failure_modes: OI conventions differ by venue (one- vs two-sided, contract units), so cross-exchange aggregation can misstate leverage; high OI alone is ambiguous — hedged and arbitrage positions inflate it without directional risk, and spot inflows can quietly lower the ratio.
misconceptions: Rising OI is not inherently bearish or bullish — it is fuel, not direction; the risk comes from OI concentration near the current price with one-sided positioning. OI is also not 'money in futures'; it is the stock of open contracts.
example: If BTC futures OI is $40B against a $1T market cap (4%), a 5% spot move forces limited liquidation flow; if OI is $120B (12%) with funding at extremes, the same move can trigger multi-billion cascades.

name: Long-short ratio
definition: The long-short ratio is the proportion of long to short positioning in a derivatives market — reported by exchanges either by account count or by position size — used as a sentiment and crowding gauge.
intuition: It is the seating chart of the derivatives arena: how many traders are on the bullish side versus the bearish side, and how lopsided the crowd has become.
mechanics: Computed as longs / shorts; e.g. a BTCUSDT ratio of 1.8145 means 1.81 long positions per short (64.5% long, 35.5% short). Venues publish variants: all accounts, top-trader positions (dollar-weighted) and top-trader accounts (count-weighted), which can diverge usefully when whales lean one way and the crowd the other. Extreme readings are often used contrarian.
formula: Long/short ratio = number (or size) of long positions / number (or size) of short positions.
failure_modes: The ratio says nothing about leverage size per account (count-based) or hedged books — a 'long' account may be hedged short elsewhere; venue-specific populations (retail-heavy Binance vs institutional CME) make cross-venue comparison meaningless.
misconceptions: A high ratio is not a bullish signal to follow — extreme one-sidedness historically precedes squeezes in the opposite direction (contrarian use). Account-count ratios also don't measure conviction; one whale can outweigh thousands of minnows in notional terms.
example: Binance BTCUSDT top-trader ratio at 2.5 (dollar-weighted) with funding at +0.05% signals crowded, leveraged longs — a setup where a small dip can trigger outsized long liquidations.

name: Cross margin
definition: Cross margin is a margin mode in which all available balance in the margin/futures account is shared as collateral across every open position, so unrealized profits and the whole account equity support each position's maintenance margin.
intuition: It is one shared life raft for all your trades: a losing position can drain the entire account to stay afloat — and if it sinks, everything goes down with it.
mechanics: Under cross margin, the account's total margin balance (wallet balance + unrealized PnL) counts toward every position's maintenance requirement, making individual positions harder to liquidate but exposing the entire account to any single failure. Leverage can be adjusted on open cross positions (on Binance); liquidation occurs when account equity falls below the maintenance margin (notional × maintenance margin rate − maintenance amount, per tier).
formula: Maintenance margin = notional position value × maintenance margin rate − maintenance amount (tiered, per Binance).
failure_modes: A single oversized losing position can consume the equity supporting every other position, turning one bad trade into a whole-account liquidation; correlated losses across positions hit the shared pool simultaneously.
misconceptions: Cross margin does not reduce risk — it redistributes it: positions are individually safer but the account as a whole is more exposed. Adding leverage across many cross positions multiplies hidden total exposure beyond any single position's setting.
example: With $10,000 in a cross account and two 5x positions of $20,000 each, a drawdown on one position is buffered by the full $10,000; but if combined maintenance margin reaches $10,000, both positions liquidate together.

name: Isolated margin
definition: Isolated margin is a margin mode in which each position carries its own dedicated collateral allotment, capping the maximum loss of that position at the margin assigned to it and ring-fencing the rest of the account.
intuition: It is a fire door between trades: each position burns with only the fuel you loaded into it, never spreading to the rest of the account.
mechanics: The trader assigns a fixed margin amount per position (and can manually add more); the position's liquidation price is computed from that isolated allotment against the maintenance margin requirement. If breached, only the isolated margin is lost — other positions and wallet balance are untouched. On Binance, leverage on open isolated positions cannot be reduced, and each isolated margin account/pair maintains its own independent risk level.
failure_modes: Isolated positions liquidate much earlier than cross positions because they lack the account buffer — a normal wick can take out the margin; over-reliance on manual margin top-ups fails exactly in fast markets when you cannot react.
misconceptions: Isolated margin limits loss per position, not total risk: running many isolated positions still sums to large account exposure. The 'cap' is the assigned margin plus any added along the way, not the initial amount if you keep topping up.
example: With $10,000 in the account, you open a 10x long with $500 isolated margin ($5,000 position); a ~10% adverse move liquidates the position for a $500 loss while the remaining $9,500 stays intact.
